utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The affirmation still applies, Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, just so there's no misunderstanding, can I suggest to you that your explanation that you went to Ovcara at -- or late evening on the 19th, that that is a lie and that in actual fact, you were at Mitnica - not Mitnica - you were at Ovcara in the afternoon when you had contact with the commander of the yellow house. You don't accept that, I know. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Good morning, Mr. Moore. First of all, I do apologise. I thought you were hurrying along. Yesterday, I thought it was time to complete your cross-examination. I thought there was no time, but I now see that there is more time. And I tried to cut some of my answers short, therefore I do have a number of additional remarks to make now that I see there is more time. You read a quote out of some newspapers that I'd never seen and -- please I will answer that one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I am putting to you, on behalf of the Prosecution, that the explanation that you gave being at Ovcara late in the evening of the 19th is not true. You were there in the afternoon. That's the only thing that I am putting to you. You have a counsel who can re-examine you on many things, I would suggest. May we move on, please. It's tab 13, tab 14, and I'm just going to read it out.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just answer? Shall I answer the question, what you read out to me that I was addressed in the army as Major Sljivancanin. It was Major, sir, in the JNA, no mention of the name. So this person who said Major and then my name just added that to add emphasis to the fact that it was me, that it was my name. As for what you said about me being at Ovcara on the afternoon of the 19th, I had been with Mr. Vance on that day until late in the day and then later on, I was with Mr. Borsinger in the hospital. And then on the 19th, on the afternoon of the 19th, I was not at Ovcara. If you have any evidence to show for that, by all means, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: From recollection, Mr. Sljivancanin, Mr. Vance was away from the Vukovar area by 2.00 in the afternoon, although you have said on previous occasions you were there until 5.00. So we will deal with document or divider or tab 13, if we may. For the English, it's page 3. But I just want to read it out. It's tab 14 for you. It's quite simply this, under B, "Teams Belgrade, Sarajevo." I just want to ask you about one entry there, "B1." It reads as follows: "On the 20th of November, 2 ECMM teams went to Vukovar via Negoslavci. They reached the centre of Vukovar at 8.45 hours and waited two hours whilst mines were cleared. The centre of the town was described as totally destroyed, occupied by bands of Serbian irregulars who were drunk and aggressive. Dead bodies were visible in the ruins." Now what I want to ask you is: Did you see bands of Serbian irregulars who were drunk and aggressive at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, you seem to be asking a number of different questions there, so please it will only be fair to allow me to answer to all the questions. You asked me questions that run into half pages or thereabouts. Again I'm telling you, Mr. Vance came for me in Negoslavci at 1400 hours on the 19th -- or left at 1400 hours. And if you look at the documents that were tendered here, you see that it was at 1400 hours. After that I went to see Mr. Mrksic. After that I looked for Mr. Borsinger. And then on the 19th, the afternoon of the 19th, I went with Mr. Borsinger to the hospital. Therefore, I was not at Ovcara. That's what you're trying to gloss over, that question persistently. So if you want to know, allow me to clarify that. As for the report, this is a report produced by other people. I know that in the town of Vukovar itself around my zone, there were the members of the Guards Motorised Brigade, there was the Vukovar TO detachment with me and within its composition was something they called a detachment. I thought it was a company actually, the Leva Supoderica. And then there was another detachment which was replaced at one point or, rather, at one point had its name changed. I thought it was the Kragujevac detachment. I didn't know that there were any other forces there, irregular forces, more specifically, that you referred to as Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am asking you a very specific question. Did you see anybody around there who was irregular, that could be described as drunk and aggressive. It's a very simple question. Did you see anybody or not on the 20th who perhaps would fit that description?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, it's a large town, a great number of people and civilians who resided there. A misfortune struck them, there were probably all sorts of things happening that those people didn't like, but I was moving about town and wherever I was, there were no such people as you have described around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you talk about size, it's right, isn't it, that the actual hospital grounds are not large, they're actually extremely small and in what I will call hospital terms. And I asked you yesterday whether you'd seen anybody who perhaps could be described as Chetnik or paramilitary. So size wasn't a problem there; was it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered your question yesterday, didn't I? It's not really such a small area; there were two buildings there. The new building, the old building and the building yard and then I moved as far as the shelter. If you want me to, I'll draw that for you, where it was near the hospital, where the command of the ZNG were and the perimeter was being secured by the military police. I know and I'm telling that you everything was perfectly in order there. You've heard witnesses who were in the hospital. Nobody complained about having been mistreated or any trouble caused them about the hospital. I didn't see, and I said that the term Chetnik is something I was taught at school. I thought it was an abominable term at the time. I didn't like those people because they fought with the Nazis and I didn't want any such terms used. What I want to use was JNA and TO. Chetnik to me is an alien term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is the term Ustasha an alien and abominable term to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that too, didn't I? Back at school, when I was a young pupil and later at the secondary school and the academy, I learned that the Ustasha sided with the Chetniks in terms of being on the same side in World War II, so it was an alien term to me. When I used the term Ustasha, I applied that term to people who used those radios to introduce themselves to each other like that by using the term Ustasha. So I used that term to apply to those people who used it themselves. I don't describe the whole of the Croatian people as Ustasha, just those who described themselves as Ustasha, just like I described myself as a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move to the morning of the 20th. Who was in the command of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I know about the progress of that situation. As a security officer, I went along with a group of security officers. I can give you their names yet again just to check whether all the security conditions at the hospital were in place to prevent any surprises and to find and single out potential perpetrators of any crimes. At the Velepromet gate, we decided that they should be taken as far as the barracks, that they should wait and the convoy should proceed for Sremska Mitrovica. They were all supposed to go to Sremska Mitrovica and then after that, the convoy for taking away the wounded and sick. Colonel Pavkovic brought those and then there was the bus convoy to take the civilians to Sid. I can't remember right now who led that convoy, but the civilian convoy that was supposed to go back to Croatia on those buses was supposed to be joining that convoy on the wounded with ambulances led by Colonel Pavkovic. Some of the wounded stayed behind in the hospital since we didn't have sufficient vehicles that day to take everybody away. As you know, they were evacuated on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why it is that colleagues of yours, military colleagues of yours, might think that you were in charge, you were the commander of that evacuation from beginning to end, i.e., Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, this is entirely untrue. Whoever says that, bring anyone, bring them on. I'll tell them straight to their face, it's a lie. I wasn't in charge of that. I should have received an order in writing for a -- verbal one, especially for a mission like that. It should have been a written order. And then for me to hold a meeting with the people who were supposed to be in charge of this or of that and then I should have planned for the use of equipment but I did none of that. All I did was the job of a security officer and I'm not shying away from that, but that was all I did. This was quite an enterprise. It took quite some planning and doing. Nor was I at any stage involved in the planning of this. Therefore, the answer is I just don't know. I think this statement is simply erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you involved or were you in charge of the evacuation of the Mitnica battalion to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in charge of that either, Mr. Moore. I explained that to you, haven't I? I told you, in my capacity as a security officer, I was required to work with my officers, use different methods and identify the perpetrators of crimes. The command of the commanders were supposed to deal with the POWs. If you see -- if you look at the rules for our security organ, there is no mention there whatsoever of POWs, not a single mention there. The only reference there is in the military police rules, it's Article 25 and Article 57. There are references there to the military police having the power to take part in the escorting of POWs, does not necessarily take part, but can. I didn't take part in that evacuation myself. I do the job of a security officer. I've described that for you. If you want me to go through that again, I will. No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In relation to the 20th, then, you say that you were involved in the selection, what I will call the triage. Who was responsible, then, for the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, as early as the evening of the 19th when I got specific tasks, security-related tasks from the commander, Colonel Mrksic, he told me that I could go and see the logistics assistant commander for him to assign me a sufficient number of vehicles to take away those who were suspects, who were suspected of committing criminal offences. That was the job that I had. I was supposed to take those crime suspects from the hospital as far as the barracks, and I put Major Vukasinovic in charge of that. I remember that he will be here to testify any way, and I can't be expected to remember every single word. I told him to get two buses. It was my assessment based on my conversations with Vesna Bosanac and Marin Vidic that maybe that many would be sufficient for the first tranche. Then I heard that two other buses were supposed to arrive because as many people would be arriving but my first assessment was two buses. So he reported and he got the two buses from the logistics assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So who got the other two buses?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Vukasinovic was in charge of that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it a case that two buses arrived on the morning of the 20th, you came to the conclusion that it wouldn't be sufficient, I say "you," I mean collectively you, and two other buses were summoned afterwards; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to go into interpreting that, perhaps I could confirm, but I think you better have Vukasinovic tell you about that. The previous evening, I thought two would be sufficient and then later on, he was in a position to ask for more, two or whatever it took. I really don't know right now. I haven't spent any time thinking about it. If two would have been sufficient or if another two buses came or if the very same two came back twice to get the people and take them there. I think he probably would be better able to explain that for you. At the time, I was with Vesna Bosanac in the office. I went to the shelter and I thought that job was in progress and I realised that it was a job that was being done in a routine fashion and strictly in keeping with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So your assessment, your initial assessment was you would have two buses or two buses would be sufficient to accommodate the number of individuals from the hospital who might interest the security organ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were people I found out that night when I was in the hospital from talking to Sergeant Jovic and the doctors who were treating people there, the medical staff and Mrs. Vesna Bosanac and Marin Vidic that they were hiding in the hospital. And they believe that they had taken part in the armed insurgency. According to us, we didn't capture them in the act of actually doing it. They had no weapons on them and for us all they were suspects. They were supposed to be taken for interrogation to Sremska Mitrovica. That evening, it may have been a misjudgement on my part, but that's how I remember it happening. I told Vukasinovic "I think two buses should do for the number of people that we are supposed to take there." I may be wrong, but that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest that you had a list of your own prior to going into the hospital on the 19th. Do you accept that, a list of people who might interest you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the list that you quoted yesterday is a list produced by the security administration for the entire territory. And you read out names from your log from the -- some other places too, that referred to the entire eastern Slavonia sector. We, as security officers, used this list in these cases. Should a person like that turn up a person who is suspected of having committed criminal offences, there was a suspicion and this person was to be taken for an interview. We didn't believe that all those people were at the hospital, nor did we believe that we would find all of them inside the hospital. Whenever a person like that was found, this person was to be taken to the Sremska Mitrovica prison, as far as their name was on the list and this person was found by us at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the selection process was going to be either from the list that you had - by the way, I don't accept that Bosanac was trying to help you to pick out individuals who fought against you - the list that you had, or the information or identification by the TO of the persons who were taken from the hospital; is that right? There were two principal sources of identification.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most principal source of identification for me and for my officers at the time was that provided by the doctors of the Vukovar Hospital and medical staff. I didn't ask about their ethnicity. Croats, Serbs, Montenegrins, Macedonians and whoever, they were just doctors for me. And they said what they said. I'm not saying that Vesna Bosanac did all of that. She said she was ready to work with us. She'd be asking the doctors to tell us who were the people who were hiding in order to not cause any trouble to the wounded. She didn't literally go from man to man picking them out saying, "That's him." And in the morning, when she had the doctors summoned, she told them to work the together with the military doctors and with us and that all those not belonging there and not medical staff should be sent away from the hospital. I'm telling you the greatest assistance we ever got in that process from anyone was from the doctors and the medical staff of the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you think of any behaviour or words that you were uttering that morning that would give people the impression that you were in charge of the evacuation, that you were the commander of the evacuation with your own officers and your own troops?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my personal opinion, I worked exceptionally well with Mrs. Vesna Bosanac and with Mr. Marin Vidic too. I was enthusiastic about the conclusions that he provided. As a human being, I saw him as a human being. He was being honest when talking about the JNA and talking about the HDZ and Tudjman. I think he was right in everything he said. If he was here, I would be glad to tell him. If you want me, I'll run that past you again. Vesna Bosanac asked me to hold a meeting to explain the situation. And then my understanding was that those peoples' understanding was because I spoke to Dr. Ivezic, Lieutenant Colonel, because he asked me for me to tell them that. I don't know why he wouldn't, since I believed him to be an important person at the hospital. I told them what I told them. If I have to say it again, I'll say it again. I think that this was the only thing that possibly could have led them to believe that I was some sort of commander. After that, there was a lot of media noise being created about my conversation with Mr. Borsinger at the bridge. And then everybody said okay, that's Major Sljivancanin, so that's my interpretation. That was the only time I gave my name to anyone or indeed focused on the fact that I was some sort of a commander. So it's not the method of work of the security officer to use fear to make people confess anything. Our method of work was a silent one, stealthy if you like, and slow. Sometimes, I'm perhaps prone to raise my voice a little, it's just a soldierly thing that I do, so that might be the impression that I make on certain people. But I'm telling you, that's the only meeting that possibly could have been the meeting that I helped with those people. And as for everything that happened in Vukovar, there was a lot of media noise being stirred up about that and directed against my person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the security organ don't use fear; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just look at the method of selection. It has been said that individuals were told either -- "and men and those who could walk to the left," is that correct? Was that said? Was that a method of selection?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room where the meeting was held, which is the room where I was, people asked questions and I explained about the groups that were there. The crime suspects who would be interrogated, who were civilians who wanted to go to the Red Cross in Sid, the civilians who were to go back to Croatia and those who wanted to remain in the hospital. And then people asked me, "Where shall we go to get our staff ready?" And then at that meeting, I may have been prompted by some people, perhaps the hospital doctors themselves. I said, "To the left, those to be interrogated at the barracks, and to the right, the hospital yard, all those split up in two groups outside that yard." That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "To the left to be interrogated at the barracks." Just out of interest, did you bring gender into it by any chance, perhaps men to the left? Or were you expecting a few women to wander down there as well?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't suspect a single woman of having committed a crime. Somehow, I didn't feel that there was any need to mention that, that any women were to be taken in. I didn't have the feeling at the time. There may have been women like that, but at the time, it's not women that I had in mind. Men were all I had in mind, and I wasn't thinking about women at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So did you or did you not say, "Men to the left, and those who can walk to the left." It's a very simple question; yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say "men" and I didn't say "those who can walk." I said, "Those who are suspected of any crimes will head left towards the gate and towards the street outside." That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If that is the case, then, can you explain how a woman came up to you and asked, "What is happening to my husband?" And you basically explained to her that, "They are going down to the barracks to be interviewed and then they would be on their way to Sremska Mitrovica," because if you're putting it out on a -- if you're indicating it in a meeting, it's not -- it's something that everybody would know, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, as I testified here, maybe as I was passing, there were people approaching me, even women to ask me questions. I didn't say at the meeting that people would be sent to the Sremska Mitrovica prison. I said for interrogation to the barracks. I didn't want to cause any more commotion, that they'd been through enough by this point. Me telling them at this point that they would be taken to prison, I don't think that was a good idea. I was trying to be humane in a way. I didn't wish to frighten them or anything. And I may have told that particular lady as I was passing that those people had been taken for interrogation to the barracks. There is no escaping that. It's a possibility. But I can't remember every single thing I said to every single person there. One thing is certain, at the meeting, I made no reference whatsoever to the Sremska Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Being the sensitive and humane man which you obviously are, is it a case, then, that you were saying to this woman to relieve her concerns that her husband was going to go to the barracks to be interrogated? Was that a phrase to relieve her concerns, Mr. Sljivancanin, as a person who might be interviewed for suspected crimes? Is that your explanation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that I said this because I didn't want to add something to all the trouble that these people were experiencing. I didn't want to say to that woman, "Oh, your husband is going to prison." In order to alleviate things, perhaps I said, "interrogation in barracks and then we would consult there." And also these women, they asked for these lists and again we returned those people who I thought were misselected. I thought that they should be released, therefore, I did not tell anyone then that they would go to prison. Whatever they asked me, I didn't say to anyone that they would be going to prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So there was no interview at the barracks, was there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in barracks. There weren't supposed to be held any in barracks. And no one was assigned to interview anyone or interrogate anyone. They were supposed to wait there for a convoy to be formed and go to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you lied to the woman; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Moore, I said how I felt then. You can interpret it any way you want. That is what you think that I lied. Her husband was perhaps among those 20 that we released ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, there were going to be no interviews. What you told this woman was a lie. That's correct, isn't it? There were no interviews. It's not a case of my interpretation. It was a lie.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a lie, because before that, women asked me to make a list -- that they would make a list of their husbands who they thought were not crime suspects, and I released a great many of them so they could return to their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, there was no interview and there was going to be no interview at the JNA barracks; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but it could have happened in that selection as I said to you, because I promised at the meeting that families would not be split up, that the people who had made this selection had made a mistake and that mistake could be corrected while they are still in barracks. The mistake could also have been rectified in Sremska Mitrovica too, so it's not a lie at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- you told the woman that her husband was going to be interviewed in the barracks. You knew there were no interviews at the barracks. That, by any standard, is a lie. For whatever reason, it is a lie, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, that's not the way I see it. These are your conclusions. I'm telling you once again, I do not know what I said to what woman, but I do know that women walked up to me, put questions to me, they asked for their husbands to be returned, those who were not perpetrators of crimes were returned. I let them make these lists, and I knew that these people would be temporarily in the barracks until the convoy was established. They would go to Sremska Mitrovica. There was always the possibility that, as I promised them at the meeting, if anyone indicates that they have information that they took the wrong man, it was possible for such a man to be released from barracks. We did everything that they asked us to do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that woman? You heard her name here. Her name was Polovina. Would it surprise you to know that there is a Polovina in the annex of the indictment? We would suggest it is her husband?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at that time, in the hospital, I did not hear that the woman's name was Polovina. I did not ask any of the women to introduce themselves to me by name and surname. If that man is indeed in the indictment, and if he indeed went missing, I am really moved, as a human being, but I really had no intention. I don't know whether Polovina or some other woman asked me. If she was the one who asked me, I really wanted to reassure her then so that she would not be stressed out. I tried my best to be fair to people and I didn't know whether her husband was in barracks or was not in barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I suggest, and I don't mean to be discourteous, please understand that, and I hope others do, that you were and are, an egotistical gentleman, who went that day controlling a situation and it was you who called that meeting, not Dr. Bosanac. You went in there in charge; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, you see, you are using very ugly words, very harsh words, and you are behaving here from positions of power. You represent a powerful world organisation that I respect. And what am I here? As a Montenegrin poet said, I'm just a straw in the whirlwinds, so what is my position? What did I try to do? I was not egotistical. I tried to help these people and I also want to bring before justice those who created commotion, trouble, who killed innocent people, soldiers, that was the law, and I strove for that. I cannot accept what you're saying now. I don't want to squabble with you. You have the right to use any words you want to use and I will always try to behave courteous and properly to you. And then it is for you to decide what kind of words you are going to use when addressing me and when speaking about me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Moore, but I am going to refer to something that he referred to in the Prosecution case. When he referred to the tone of Mr. Borovic's question put to one of the Prosecution witnesses. Of course I don't mind that Mr. Moore puts questions related to the facts, but in terms of qualifications like this, comments on Mr. Sljivancanin's personality, those are facts that can only be part of a second part of a question, the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you finished with that matter, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest, perhaps if I put it this way, you refer to Montenegrins being a straw in the wind. The second time you have mentioned Montenegro. You are from Montenegro. Obviously, it's a gross generalisation, but would it be fair to say that Montenegrins can be plain speaking people? You are not the only one in this court who is from Montenegrin, but would that be a trait?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're interested in what Montenegrins are like, I have a book here in prison that was written by a German author who spent quite a bit of time with Montenegrins and he described the people there. I can bring it for you tomorrow and I can give it to you. You can read it. I really don't want to talk about that now. I think that we are a civilised people, normal people. I cannot denounce my origins. I was brought up the way I was brought up. I am the way I am. It would be best for you to come to Montenegro and to spend a bit of time with Montenegrins and you will see that we are normal people just like anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on to the actual evacuation itself. Who was in charge of the buses and the transfer of Ovcara people?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What kind of transfer of Ovcara and when did this occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The people who were taken from the hospital, I often called them the Ovcara people or the Ovcara victims, the people who were taken from the hospital and eventually ended up at the JNA barracks and then went on, minus some individuals at Ovcara, who was in charge of the transportation of them? Who was in charge of the control of the individuals?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were in hospital and who were suspected of having committed crimes and who were to be taken to the barracks, Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic was in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who supplied the soldiers on the buses?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, soldiers for securing these buses were from the 2nd Battalion of the military police commanded by Major Radomir Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you have any discussion with Paunovic that morning at the hospital about what was to be achieved or indeed any discussion with him about these individuals being removed from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I talked to Paunovic on the afternoon of the 19th and I talked to him on the morning of the 20th. He was there. As far as I can remember, there was a company commander of his there too. I saw the two of them. They said that the night was peaceful and that there was nothing going on. And I said that what would be done then would be the work that we came there for and that his soldiers would be helping. Those were the tasks and the jobs that he had, normal police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the important thing to bear in mind, I would suggest, is that you have a double function here. You are responsible for the triage, as you call it, but you are also commander of the security organ within the zone of responsibility of the 1st Motorised Brigade, Guards Motorised Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I was not a commander, I was the chief of the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you still had a function as chief of the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade. That task still subsisted; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was chief of security of the Guards Brigade when I was there in hospital. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the barracks were within the zone of responsibility of the Guards Motorised Brigade; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks were within the zone of responsibility of the Guards Motorised Brigade. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And criminal behaviour or acts is a matter of concern to the security organ; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, security organs take part in these tasks, but crimes are something that everyone has to deal with, soldiers, commanders, the military police, crime prevention, control, resolving these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will ask the question again. Criminal behaviour or criminal acts are a matter of concern to the security organ; that is correct, isn't it? It may well be other officers as well, we can deal with that later on, but for the security organ, it is one of your areas of concern; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the tasks in which the security organs participate as well. Yesterday we interpreted the rules. Now I don't really want to interpret it the way it suits you. I want to give the interpretation that the regulations stipulate. Now we explained that very nicely yesterday. Where they are the mainstays of certain things and where they participate in certain matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The answer went too fast. The interpreter did not catch the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were told by Vukasinovic -- Your Honour, it's very difficult to know how to deal with it. Mr. Sljivancanin, you're talking rather quickly sometimes. The interpreter, I think, failed to get the last part of the answer and I'll read it to you. And it's the last part of the answer if you can just expand although I don't think it will change much. "One of the tasks in which the security organs participate as well, yesterday, we interpreted the rules. Now, I don't really want to interpret it the way it suits you, I want to give the interpretation that the regulations stipulate. Now we explained that very nicely yesterday. Where they are the mainstays of certain things and where they participate in certain matters." That is all that is recorded. Is there anything else that you want to add to that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise to the interpreters and to you, sir, if I went too fast. I don't want to repeat myself, that's why I'm hurrying, but I will be patient enough to speak slower. Yesterday, when we discussed the rules and regulations, we said what the main tasks were or, rather, where the organs of the -- security organs were the mainstays, the protagonists. And there is this other group of tasks which they participate like other officers, commands and so on and they are not the ones who are in charge of these tasks; they participate, they assist therein. One of these tasks where they participate is crime prevention and control and finding the perpetrators of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you were told by Vukasinovic that there had been problems at the barracks; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my best to be precise. Vukasinovic, when he brought a group of people that I had asked to be returned, after having talked to the women, which is what you asked me about, he said that certain members of the Territorial Defence, as he was taking these people out of the buses to take them back, they tried to abduct some of these people. And they were making noise, so to speak. They were cursing, they were saying ugly things about them, shouting at them. There were also a group of members of the Territorial Defence who had gathered near the barracks and they were asking why I was setting these people free, these 24 who were on that list. Now, that is what Vukasinovic said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you are referring to abduction, abduction means taking away; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not taking them away. It was my understanding that they were moving towards these people that Vukasinovic had singled out -- that's what I meant, that they did not abduct anyone because the military police was there so that was prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suspect this is a problem on translation. What you said was, "They tried to abduct some of these people." What I'm suggesting to you, it's not a case of just words, there was an attempt to remove people, so it was an extremely serious situation. The removal of people who were suspected of committing criminal acts against Serbs. That's the point. It's not just words, it's the attempt to remove people that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think differently, and I thought differently then too. There were always some frustrated people in that town, people who had experienced many traumas, people who lived through that, this interethnic conflict. It was not easy. And now, in that nervousness, one could -- a person could get very upset, perhaps somebody recognised a neighbour, whoever, I don't know. But I know that nothing happened to these people and as I had requested, all of the people who were on the list were returned to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they had tried to mistreat the people whom you had extracted. These are very benign words, "mistreat." Did you ever ask, Well, what were they trying to do? Were they hitting them? Were they beating them?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When these people came, Vukasinovic informed me that he did not allow anyone to approach them, and none of these people who were brought in had been hurt and none of them complained to me that they had been beaten. I'm telling you again, there were frustrated people in town, especially these civilians who were there in town and then finally when the town was free and when they could move about, some people saw destroyed houses, some had somebody close to them killed. So of course it was our suspicion that people could feel frustrated in that kind of situation and could be saying all sorts of things. And most often they were saying to them that they were Ustashas, they were cursing them, using these swear words that I remember Vukasinovic told me about then. Well, such things did happen among the population, yes. That wasn't new. Nothing was ideal there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm asking you, and as I suggested yesterday, there was a possibility of revenge; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was convinced, and I am convinced now as well that where these officers were, the ones that I had assigned different tasks or where the officers of the Guards Motorised Brigade were, that no retaliation could take place. We did our best to take correct measures and to protect and shield people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I respectfully suggest to you that is complete nonsense because many of these people in the TO were armed and were perfectly capable of shooting someone. This was not an unarmed group of people completely, was it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that members of the Territorial Defence were armed and from day one, there was this situation until we introduced law and order. On one occasion, Colonel Mrksic even issued an order to the Colonel. He said, If necessary, you can trample upon them with tanks but they are not going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, the question is perfectly straightforward. It's not a case of just words. You had a group of frustrated individuals, some of them TO, some of them who might have lost loved ones, who were armed and attacking the bus or attempting to attack the bus; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard what people said here while they were giving evidence, but I was not in barracks, so it's not for me to conclude whether it was that way or whether it was not that way or whether people are adding things, but the fact remains that nothing happened to anyone in the barracks. I am giving you my word that I am sure that the guards would have used tanks and weapons and anything and they would have prevented the Territorial Defence from doing anything if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And yesterday or the day before, you indicated to this Court you did nothing to contact anyone at the barracks to see whether the situation was deteriorating; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, you always draw some kind of conclusions that you want to draw. That is your opinion. That's not what I said. So please, read that page to me. I don't know. Perhaps I spoke very fast and I just spoke too fast. I asked Vukasinovic who was there. I asked him, Is Colonel Panic there? And he said, Yes. Is lieutenant Colonel Lukic there? Yes, that was the commander of the barracks or, rather, the commander of the garrison. Knowing those officers, that is not secret work on the part of security organs. One knows what discipline is. The security organ does not resolve this discipline. It is for the command to resolve that. If they were there, I was convinced and I am convinced today that they would take measures and they would resolve the question of discipline and they would improve the discipline. That was my position then and that is what I said to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You had a radio, you had individuals at your disposal, you never sent Vukasinovic back to clarify the situation and you never made any radio attempt to see what was happening at the barracks; that is the fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I gave my answer yesterday. As for this radio communication I had, I had it with Negoslavci, not with the barracks, but with the building where I was, with my desk officers, so that they could send a message to me if necessary, and things like that. Again, I'm telling you, as for the chain of command, it was not my duty to introduce order and discipline in barracks. It was not for me to give assignments to officers. The officers who were in barracks are going to come and testify and they are going to explain what the order was in barracks. At that time, I did not think it was necessary, if responsible officers in barracks were there, that I was supposed to caution them about something. It was the day-to-day duty of the commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's much more than that, because the people who were sent back on your suggestion when they came with Vukasinovic, Vujevic was with you on the re-selection at the hospital. And I think you told us that in actual fact, that there were individuals in that re-selected group who indicated that they had killed some people and they said who it was they had killed. And as a consequence of that, they were, as it were, re-apprehended. So you had people who actually admitted, so you say, had admitted murdering or killing individuals; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, when those people were returned to the hospital compound, there were journalists there, there were EC monitors there, even Mr. Vujevic came with some TO men and addressed me, saying, that he knew that the people whom I was about to release were perpetrators of criminal offences and I said, That's up to you. And then I took some people outside the hospital who knew those people and I called the MPs who were there. For example, I read out the name of this particular person, he responds. I say, Does anyone know what this man did? And I ask Vujevic, Do you know if there were any criminal offences that he committed? You are from the area, so you should know. And he said, I heard he was a member of the HDZ. And I said to him, Well, you were a party member too of some party, rather, right? This man wasn't carrying a gun, he wasn't shooting. So he's leaving with his family and that's that. Those four people who remained said themselves, We shot at people and we killed some people. And they told us about some people they killed at a petrol station in front of everybody there in the hospital, and I had no doubts any longer. I told Vukasinovic, Take these people to the Sremska Mitrovica prison. That's where they should go and that was all the selection that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest that is complete and utter nonsense that four men would confess to killing or murder to you or the TO and that you are using that as a means to justify them getting back on that bus. That's what I'm suggesting to you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, you weren't there. How can you possibly know? What you're saying, again, you can say whatever you like, but I'm telling you from the depths of my soul, the very truth, what we experienced. I even admired that particular commander, Mitar Karaula, who was -- I admired his honesty, he honour. It doesn't matter that we were enemies. He was an honourable man. So, Your Honours, that's what I'm trying to say, there were people -- allow me to answer this, please. Allow me to answer this question. There were honourable Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This is about four people you say confessed to killing, to murder, in front of the TO commander and yourself, the TO commander objecting that they were being released because he knew they were killers. I'm suggesting it's complete nonsense, it's not about Karaula?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people too, quite specifically, Mr. Moore, it's not nonsense at all. There were people who regretted their actions, who were proud and who were honourable, perhaps, and they said there right on the spot, I did this or I did that. Either, among those people who were sent back, there were people who said we have mobilised by force and we were just there to take food to these ZNG men, but we didn't shoot or use a weapon. I didn't believe that such people should be taken away as crime perpetrators. I felt that most of the people there were telling the truth; that's the feeling I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move off from this topic, but the situation was that you were told that there were TO members up at the barracks. Now, let us move on. It's right to say that you, at no time, knew about a government meeting until you returned to Negoslavci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first I heard about the government meeting was what I heard from my desk officer Srecko Borisavljevic when I came to Negoslavci. I had not known of that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the answer to that question was yes.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that government meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's right to say when you heard about it, you were surprised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's also right to say that one of your other security organs, Mr. Karanfilov, told you that day about the incidents at the JNA barracks when the buses were attacked. That is correct also, isn't it? You've not given that in evidence, but I'm suggesting it to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Karanfilov. I told him to bring Marin Vidic to that shelter where the ZNG were on that day, that afternoon, but I don't remember talking to him about the barracks at all. I simply can't remember. I don't remember, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm suggesting to you that Karanfilov told you about the violence at the JNA barracks that day.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you're saying. I never heard Karanfilov utter anything like that. I don't remember. The only thing I heard is what I was told by Major Vukasinovic at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov is allegedly one of your witnesses and I have a statement from him and I'm suggesting to you that is what he said when that statement was taken. Might he be right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karanfilov will take the stand. We'll hear his story. As for these words, him telling me about acts of violence committed, I simply don't remember. I can't even remember that we talked about the barracks. We talked about his mission, the mission that he'd been assigned but I told him nothing in relation to the barracks and I gave him no tasks in relation to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you went to Negoslavci, you saw Vukasinovic again and he told you that he had been to Ovcara with this group of people who had been taken from the barracks; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukasinovic told me he had been informed by Captain Predojevic and this had originally come from the brigade command to the effect that the last group that he had brought was now to be taken to Ovcara because that was the conclusion that no one should now stay at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is right to say that Vukasinovic told you that the people had been taken to Ovcara. That is what surprised you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It surprised me, sure enough. I knew people were to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica, so yes, I was surprised by that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I will read what you have said in evidence: "He found the other people from the barracks there and members of the TO including Miroljub Vujevic. He said they were behaving - how should I put it - violently." So you have got Vujevic having an incident with you at the hospital where, I believe, I think it's right, that he raised a gun towards you, but certainly he was objecting to individuals being removed. And here, you are being told by Vukasinovic that those people were now at Ovcara, the same man was there, and the TO were behaving violently. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, it's true, Vukasinovic said that the TO men had again tried to act in a frustrated and violent way. He said he'd met Vujevic there and had warned him about this. Vujevic allegedly reacted and restored order to that scene. He also told me that the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade then arrived and took over securing those people who were where they had previously been brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you had been told that they had been behaving violently. Did you ask him, What do you mean violently?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I asked him. He said foul language, calling out names, threats being made, you murderers, that sort of thing. Those were the words that I heard. I can't be expected to repeat every single word I heard, but it struck me as very frustrated people calling other people names such as Ustasha and that sort of thing. That's what I remember, the words being used and what Vukasinovic told me in terms of what sort of language was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect to you, Mr. Sljivancanin, violently in normal usage does not mean saying nasty words to people, it tends to mean physical acts of violence.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, well, that depends on your take on it, doesn't it? That's what I took it to mean, insults, taunts. I didn't understand Vukasinovic to be saying that they had been physically attacked, since the military policemen from the 80th Motorised Brigade had already set up a security system. I'm telling you that was my impression at the time. I wasn't physically present at the scene, but that was the impression that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told this Court what a noble and decent man you are and your concerns. Were you concerned for the welfare of those people at Ovcara when you heard that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was concerned throughout. The idea of violent behaviour was totally alien to me. We were all concerned. And that's why eventually I went to see the commander to see what our further tasks would be and then Major Vukasinovic told me that he had informed the commander of all these things so those were no longer secret missions for intelligence bodies. The chain of command was well-known. And he told me that Lieutenant Colonel Panic had been there too. So my understanding was these were perfectly normal, simple tasks. If there was anything that was known, it was all known and it was normal. And security would now be taken over by a fresh well-rested unit. They were in charge of the area and there could be no further riots or anything there. That was my understanding then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I asked you the question, "Were you concerned for the welfare of those people at Ovcara when you heard that?" And you replied, "I was concerned throughout." Does that reply, "I was concerned throughout," run from the hospital through the day? Is that concern an ongoing concern?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're adding something to what I said about my own opinion. I said I was concerned throughout. I meant the area of combat operations. Throughout, from day one, until the very end. I tried to make sure that all that misfortune, whoever was free to still be safe and for conditions to be ensured for people to get on with their lives to the extent that they could. From the hospital to the barracks, there were officers in charge of certain tasks and I believe those officers to be capable, perfectly capable of carrying out their tasks in a regular manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I asked you about the people at Ovcara. I was specifically targeting that group. When you heard from Vukasinovic the first time you've given your reply, you've heard now Vukasinovic telling you about violence, were you concerned about the welfare of those people from Ovcara or at Ovcara. What is your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that Vukasinovic had informed me about him establishing full control and that security was now in the charge of the military policemen of the 80th Motorised Brigade, my conclusion was that people were safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were not concerned?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't particularly concerned. I knew that the police were there, the unit was there, the commanders were there. I knew that people would now be safe, there was nothing out of hand, there was nothing that was not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you indicated you were going to tell Mrksic about it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to see Mrksic to tell him what I'd seen at the hospital, and what happened at the hospital that day and to see what would be further tasks and duties. Vukasinovic had previously told me, when he had returned from Mitnica, he went to see Mrksic and met him -- or, rather, informed him about all of that. And since the chief of staff, Mr. Panic was there, I believed them to be in the know in the sense of knowing exactly what was going on why those people had gone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was it your intention to tell Mrksic about not only the hospital but also the JNA barracks, the behaviour there, and the behaviour at Ovcara towards those prisoners? Was that your intention when you were intending to go and speak to him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I thought the chain of command and the commanders were informing people about what had been going on, and everything. I wasn't in charge of the barracks myself. I wasn't in charge of discipline since the barracks actually had a commander. I believed that Mrksic was in touch with the commander. I had no possibility of reminding Mrksic or the barracks commander all the time about what their duties were. Any officer doing all of that would not have been a mere chief of security. Since all of the commanders and officers were in place, I simply took it for a fact that everything was going smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So does that mean you were not going to tell Mrksic about the attacks at the barracks and you were not going to tell Mrksic about the attacks at Ovcara? Now what is the straight answer on this, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I didn't hear of any attacks. Again, at the time, I had no task in relation to the barracks or Ovcara, for that matter. The officers who were there were supposed to report on anything that went on and anything to do with those tasks. It's difficult to say, off the bat, I would be lying to the Chamber and I would be lying to you if I said everything that you are suggesting I should say. I can't remember every single thing that crossed my mind at the time. I went to see the commander to ask him why those people had gone to Ovcara and not to Sremska Mitrovica and to tell him about what had been done at the hospital for as long as I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "So I went to see the commander to ask him why these people had gone to Ovcara," yes, "not to Sremska Mitrovica, and to tell him what had been done at the hospital." Is that because you knew from Vukasinovic that Vukasinovic had told Mrksic about the threats at the JNA barracks and the violence, as you've described, at Ovcara; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well simply because I knew that those people were to go to Sremska Mitrovica. Based on what Vukasinovic had told me, I was now surprised that they were taken to Ovcara. Instead I didn't know what was going on or what they were there for. As for what Srecko Borisavljevic told me, he told me that they had been at a government meeting and that was a surprise for me too simply because I never believed that any such government should exist and that's a political issue and it's not my place to discuss that. He told me that Bogdan Vujic had told him that there had been some mistreatment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I'm dealing with the state of knowledge that you had at that time and the information that had been given to Mrksic. Now, you say that Borisavljevic had spoken to Mrksic. Did Borisavljevic -- I beg your pardon, Vukasinovic had spoken to Mrksic. Had Vukasinovic had said to Mrksic that he had told him about the behaviour at the barracks and the behaviour at Ovcara. That's all I want to know, it's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I learned from Vukasinovic that day, I think he informed Colonel Mrksic about what had happened at Ovcara. My understanding was correct, that order was restored and that the people were there. I don't know whether he talked to him about the barracks that day. I can't be expected to remember every single little thing. You asked me why I went to see Mrksic and that's precisely what I am trying to explain, because of what he told me, when he told me about those people going to Ovcara and not to Mitrovica. And also because of that, because of what Bogdan Vujic had told Srecko Borisavljevic, that someone from higher up had given orders for those people to be taken over or surrendered to the government. So I went to see the commander whether that was in fact true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just look at this reply you've given. Vukasinovic said he told Mrksic and Mrksic said nothing. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that Mrksic said nothing. All I said is Vukasinovic told me that after coming back from Ovcara, he had informed the commander about what had gone on at Ovcara and that Lieutenant Colonel Panic was present too. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, your evidence was as follows: "After this," this is Vukasinovic, "After this, he went back to the command post and informed Colonel Mrksic about all of this. He said Mrksic told him nothing." 13663: 22 is the reference. Mrksic told him nothing. That was your evidence.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that. Perhaps that should be read back. It may be a slip of the tongue or a misinterpretation, but I really don't remember Vukasinovic telling me Mrksic told me nothing. I was surprised. I was just listening to all of this. I was surprised that all those people had been taken to Ovcara and not to Mitrovica. I don't remember him telling me he told me nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you then went to see Mrksic because you wanted to report to him about what had happened at the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I wanted to tell about what I had done in the hospital, what I had done with the shelter, the tasks I was performing, and how many people were still left in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did it concern you that Vukasinovic had told you that Mrksic had said nothing about potential threats and acts of violence towards the Ovcara individuals?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that, haven't I? I don't remember Vukasinovic telling me that Mrksic had told him nothing. All I was surprised at -- I can't remember every single word that was exchanged. Vukasinovic will be coming along, so we'll ask him, won't we? I was surprised that the people were taken from the barracks to Ovcara, rather than to Sremska Mitrovica. That was what caused my surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you went to see Colonel Mrksic, did you tell him about the threats at the barracks and the account that Vukasinovic had given you about what had been happening at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn’t… we didn’t talk. I didn’t repeat what Vukasinovic had told me. And we did not talk about the threats. This was a spontaneous conversation. I called in, I don’t know if Mr. Mrksic too was in a hurry then, but time was short. And I told him that the convoy carrying the wounded had set out, that they were done there, that we cleared the shelter for booby-traps, that all the equipment had been taken away and sent to Belgrade, as far as I remember. As I was talking, Mrksic said what I said to you, what was said here and then if necessary, I can repeat that for you. During that conversation or dialogue, Mrksic said that there had been a government meeting, that our Guards Brigade would now be going off to get some rest and that the 80th Motorised Brigade would be taking over responsibility, that the government took charge of some of the people back in the barracks in order to have been exchanged for their own Serbs. And that was the end of that conversation. It was at this point that it dawned on me that those people from the barracks had been taken away and had been taken to Ovcara because of that. I believed that those people would be taken from there somewhere else, that they would not be held at Ovcara, that they would be taken to some centre because, to begin with, there was no proper conditions in place at Ovcara for holding people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Mrksic say to you that that day, he had been contacted by Susic who was at the barracks and had telephoned him to warn he, Mrksic, about the behaviour at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrksic didn't say anything else that evening, apart from that. He said, Go and see General Vasiljevic. Go get some rest. He said he would be going to Belgrade the next day and he said the next morning, I should see Colonel Panic to give him a hand and to set up security for the press conference in Vukovar the next day. But Mrksic was in no way duty bound to report to me what the battalion commander had told him and what they had done. This is above the chain of command. He is a commander that was not supposed to report to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've asked you a very simple question. Did Mrksic say he knew about it from Susic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything about Susic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he say that he knew about it from Panic, because Panic had been at Ovcara and had witnessed the beatings?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Panic was seated right there at headquarters and he made no reference to Panic whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he say that he had been contacted by Tomic who had expressed concerns about what was happening at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything about Tomic, nor do I remember that name at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did he say that he had spoken or been spoken to by Vukasinovic about the concerns and did nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I remember him telling me. I don't remember anybody else being mentioned by the commander, nor did he submit any reports to me as to any reports that have been submitted to him, simply because he wasn't required to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid the transcript is running away from us. Page 38, line 21, the witness said that Mr. Mrksic had told him that he would be going to Belgrade and the transcript said that Mrksic told him that he would be going to Belgrade the next day, so this is not something the witness said, he only told him that he would be off to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal, if I may, please, with General Vasiljevic. You were told that General Vasiljevic wanted to speak to you as a matter of urgency and you then went and telephoned him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I phoned the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as your evidence is is that General Vasiljevic was concerned about some documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, the previous evening, when General Vasiljevic was with us on our premises, the evening of the 19th, we informed him about what we had, what we had collected, documents, letters. And I told him that we had not been able to get all the documents from the commander's shelter because the shelter was booby-trapped. I said that we would do it the next day with the assistance of the engineers. And he said I was supposed to send these documents to the chief of security of the cabinet. And then he said that he would talk to him that evening because of the importance and priority of this matter for that to be sent to him directly to the security administration because certainly this was by all means to reach the chief of security of the cabinet at the administration. He said he'd see to this with Jukic and that I shouldn't worry about this. And this one time that he said he called me, I said I don't remember. I haven't completed my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that evening, when I phoned, he picked up the phone -- or, rather, General Vasiljevic didn't pick up the phone immediately, maybe it was the Colonel who was on duty and maybe he conveyed to me the request of General Vasiljevic or maybe he put me through. I just can't remember. He did ask me though to quickly send through whatever it was that we had and I said it's already on its way to you. It was sent that afternoon before nightfall when we had pulled out from that shelter, whatever we were able to, and that was the extent of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's what I want to ask you about. Here you are, you have got a government meeting that you don't actually think should even exist. You have got a group of individuals who have been routed away from their intended route itself. You have got indications of possible violence, putting it mildly, and you have a commander saying, Our task is done. Why didn't you tell Vasiljevic, General or comrade General, what is going on here? I don't know what's going on and I am the chief of the security organ. Did you mention to General Vasiljevic these problems just so that he could give you one of his pearls of wisdom, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I told you that I wasn't sure whether I talked to General Vasiljevic that evening or the Colonel on duty; however, since the General on the previous evening said to me that all questions related to security, I can fully accept all the demands made by Colonel Vujic who came from the security administration with those tasks. According to the information given to me by Srecko Borisavljevic, Vujic had been at the government meeting, he was present all the time, he was present in the barracks when these people were taken over by the government. I believed then -- well, if I knew everything I know now, and the advice you are giving me is very wise advice, I would have been the happiest man in the world if I would have thought of that then and if I had sacrificed my own life and if I released all those people and even if I would be court-martialed as a traitor in my own army, but if I released all of them and in this way saved their lives. But I believe that if Vujic was there and the security people were there, the people knew. And I did not give any kind of advice to the General or to the Colonels because they were on the spot and they were resolving things. And when the commander said to me that this government was in session and that it was agreed that they would take over these people, I thought that all of this had been agreed upon normally. Then I thought that perhaps they needed to exchange their own people, that's what crossed my mind then. I really didn't discuss it. I wish I had all the experience then that I have now and then perhaps I would have acted differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that mean the answer is "no"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is not no. The answer is the answer I gave you. I gave you an extensive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a good time, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a technical matter. I talked to Mr. Moore during the break. He cannot say anything in very strict terms, but he thinks that he will finish with his cross-examination around the next break, perhaps a bit before that, perhaps after that, he said. I would have about 35 minutes to 40 minutes for my redirect, so I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber for permission to release our next witness so that we don't keep him here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, we then resume with another witness at 10.00 tomorrow. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, 1995 was a period when you were aware that an indictment had been issued against you from this Tribunal; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I was in Podgorica and, as far as I remember, I was out in the field near Herceg Novi between Herceg Novi and Dubrovnik and then I read in the newspapers that an indictment had been issued against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And clearly you were appalled at such an allegation and presumably, you made inquiries to see what the basis of the allegation was against you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like any normal person, I was absolutely astonished because I remembered what I had learned in schools, that only SS officers were tried, having been charged with aggression against different countries and the fascism that they had perpetrated. It was hard for me to see myself in that kind of group of people. I was a person in my own country and I asked the army commander for permission to be received by the Chief of General Staff of the then army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that you were aware that Mr. Mrksic was also indicted as well as Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I read about that in the newspapers, that this indictment had been issued against the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it also correct to say that you were subsequently informed, presumably by some authorities, that it really dealt with the murder of individuals at the Ovcara farm?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was received by the Chief of General Staff, of course I had to wait for a long time, quite a bit of time had to go by before that happened. As far as I can remember now, he told me then that he had read about that in the newspapers, too, that he had not received any official notification about that, that he did not believe that that kind of thing could have been done by the officers of the Guards Brigade and that there is no evidence against us, but that he would seek whatever was in -- within the realm of his possibilities, that matter be fully investigated, that I should normally go on with my duties, of course, that I should be concerned, that he would take all measures to investigate that and that he personally would ask to see me and talk to me again when the need arose for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's right, isn't it, and it's logical that you would ask: Well, what is it I'm supposed to have done? Where has this occurred? I want to know details. Isn't that what you wanted to know?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to contact many people in order to gather information who were not serving together with me then, who were in different garrisons then, but we all served in Vukovar together. But we were all astonished because we knew that at that time we were not aware of a crime, we had not heard of a crime and we could not believe that that kind of crime could have happened. It never crossed our minds that something like that could have happened. First of all, I was concerned as to whether, perhaps, people had been killed who were taken prisoner at Mitnica. I never thought of the people from the hospital because I thought that the government had taken those people and exchanged them, as I was told then.
