And I was checking the list of names of persons in Mitnica who surrendered with weapons and I did not see any of those names mentioned in the newspapers. Then I thought whether it was the civilians from Croatia, whether they were returned to Ovcara, and then I did not see on that list -- at first there weren't any women's names and I quite simply could not believe it, in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just try and narrow it down. You thought it might be Mitnica, it wasn't Mitnica. So then you thought might it be -- sorry, did you think it might be people from the hospital? If it wasn't Mitnica, it had to be another group.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't think of it then because I believed that if these people were handed over to serious people to be exchanged for their prisoners, I think that everyone then strove for the end of this violence to have this exchange carried out and I really did not think that these people had been killed. I thought that they had been exchanged. That is what I thought then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well if I deal with it then fairly quickly, you didn't have any suspicion it might be the hospital people, it might have been some other group; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't have a shade of doubt along those lines, that these people had been killed, those who were taken to be exchanged. I thought it was a great virtue to save a single human life at least, and to establish peace in that territory because again we have to live together, geographically, and in any way, we simply cannot survive without each other and I simply thought that these people had been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before you went for your interviews in Belgrade in 1998, therefore, you were not aware that there was the suggestion that it was the people from the hospital who had been killed; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told you I didn't know about that. There were different rumours in the newspapers, these people killed, those people killed, but I did not know that it was that group. I really thought that that group had been exchanged. That is what I thought then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've got two files created or I've created two files. I'd like to hand those out now, please. Thank you. Now, what I want to do, again, it's exactly the same format as I've used in the past. There is an index, four tabs, one, two, three and four, English, B/C/S. I want to deal, if I may, please, with tab 1, English, tab 2, B/C/S. This is a publication. It's called, "Monitor". It's a Montenegrin newspaper or publication; isn't that right? It's tab 2 for you, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. Mr. Moore, that is true, there is this newspaper that is published in Montenegro by that name, but it's a tabloid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And it is -- it describes an interview with Lieutenant Colonel Veselin Sljivancanin, Yugoslav army 1st Motorised Brigade Chief of Staff, headline, "Why I razed Vukovar to the ground." A gentleman called Vladimir Jovanovic. Now, I want to deal with certain parts. Now, I want to go, if I may, please --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something about this interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, you've got a splendid barrister defending you and I'm sure he will be able to deal with it. But for the moment, I'd like to deal with the question and answer scenario. Now, the first question is from monitor, sir: "You have probably heard about the report of a UN special rapporteur, for human rights on the fate of about 175 patients of the Vukovar Hospital." Note the word "patients" and note the word "Vukovar Hospital." "On the 20th of November last year, i.e., after the liberation. Many of them were taken out of the hospital by the back door while you stood in front of it and prevented the ICRC representatives from entering, saying, 'This is my land.' What do you know about all of that, about the crimes and mass graves?" This is what they say was your answer: "I know a lot about those events and I want to speak openly and objectively. First during the liberation of Vukovar, I maintained that all Europeans were against Serbia, the Serbian people and the army. They did not want to listen to many positive things. Second, it was clear what they really wanted. They wanted to force the Serbian and Montenegrin peoples to their knees. To this day, the Europeans have not mentioned the suffering of the Serbian people. I am convinced - I know for sure - that we from the guard unit treated everybody in accordance with international law. We formed columns of people according to the following criteria: We first wanted to take care of the women and children and then the rest. We sent the columns to Croatia but the Croats returned the people the same day. So, we simply did not have the opportunity to take care of them. Some of the prisoners and other people attempted to escape through the cornfield at night." "Furthermore, a few people who belonged to the other population group attempted to do things. You know, somebody's house had been blown up so they wanted revenge, to kill or mutilate people. But as long as we controlled the situation, nothing happened. I am not sure that were any mass graves. Well, we sent 50 buses to Vinkovci which was about 20 kilometres away and they returned them. They said to the people, 'Let the army feed you.' Well, I don't have that much room and facilities. We let them sleep in the building and houses and did not bother them because they had been disarmed." Dealing with this very first issue, I suggest there is reference to patients, there's reference to hospital, and the fact that there are missing people from the hospital. Now, do you accept that you had an interview with "Monitor"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, first of all, you read a lot out and this went public and you didn't allow me to explain anything. I am telling you that this is an invented interview. As for the gentleman who wrote this interview, at the request of the then chief of information of the general staff, his name was General Bavcar [phoen]; I remember that. He was my professor at the military academy too. Mr. Bavcar called me and said, Sljivancanin, since you're a Montenegrin, a man from the Montenegrin newspaper is asking you for an interview. Please receive him and talk to him. And I said: Oh, please don't, there have been plenty of interviews, there's enough of that. I don't really want to talk about anything. So in order not to explain this at great length, he was my professor, after all, I did receive him. When I received this man, he was so full of hatred against me. All of these are his words. I simply did not want to give him an interview. I said to him, sir, if my General tells me to give you an interview, I will give you an interview. Go write up your questions, bring your questions, I'm going to answer your questions in writing and then I want to authorise the interview. We chatted a bit off the record, and he went away, promised that he would write up these questions. He never came. He never brought his questions, and then he published this interview. If you wish to read it out, read it out. If necessary, bring the journalist in here. Let us confront each other and let us see whether this is my interview. I do not accept this interview as my own. Perhaps some of the words do come from the chat that we had but this is something that he compiled without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's see about the material that you said you had a chat with him. When you had a chat with him, did you maintain that all Europeans were against Serbia, the Serbian people and the army?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are his words. I never claimed that. To this day, I am a civilised person belonging to a civilised people. We like other people. We like to extend hospitality to other people. We received everyone nicely. I talk to everyone and I never claimed that people were against Serbia and the Serbian people. Everybody, of course there are some who are against, but I always speak up if I feel that somebody is against someone or something, as I said to my friend Borsinger, when I said what happened to my soldiers, but we still remained friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We'll talk about your friendship with Mr. Borsinger in a moment, but did he mention to you about the fate of patients from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this man who came to see me, came filled with hatred towards the Yugoslav People's Army, and he was saying that I was a Serb. There is no hesitation in my mind and I was born in Montenegro and I've always known that and when I was first asked in Sarajevo at secondary school what my ethnicity was, I said I was a Montenegrin and I always said that freely -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I asked you very simply, did he mention about patients from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, after all these years, I do not remember all the things that he mentioned to me. But this is an invented interview. The gentleman did not bring it to me to authorise it and all of these are not my words. There's nothing more for me to say. He attacked me, he insulted me when he came to see me and he expressed that hatred through this interview. Bring this gentleman here to testify and let me question him and let my lawyers question him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, we couldn't let you interview him. Now could I just deal, please, with the Vukovar Hospital. Did he or did he not mention it to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember because I was so upset because of the way he approached me. I didn't even listen to everything he was saying. I said bring your concrete questions, I will give you concrete answers and then we'll have it authorised. He never came. And he published this "interview" and, regardless of all the bad things he did, vis-a-vis me -- I mean he talked to me for five or ten minutes and then he wrote this up and he put his own words in, whatever suited him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you say, "To this day, the Europeans have not mentioned the suffering of the Serbian people"? Was that not a view that you took at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my view and, as a matter of fact, I had good relations with many people from Europe that I met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, did he correctly report, "I know that for sure that we from the guards unit treated everybody in accordance with international law." That was your view, wasn't it, that you in the guards unit had treated everybody properly?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said here many times until now that I truly am convinced. Whatever I managed to learn, the members of the Guards Brigade -- well, I'm not talking about each and every individual because there are always people that are not as good as the rest but I did not know that members of the Guards Brigade doing anything that was not correct and that was not consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I want to move on. I said to Mr. Lukic we're try to finish this session. Please keep your answers short if you can. Is it right that you said, moving on down, "... that a few people who belonged to the other population group, attempted to do things, you know, somebody's house being blown up, so they wanted revenge to kill or mutilate people." Did you mention the fact that there was behaviour that might generate revenge?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I am speaking very frankly all the time. And now that you mention this interview, when I first saw it published, I was horrified and I actually sought the man many times because I wanted to see him and speak to him. And from the editorial desk of "Monitor" they actually offered me what they call the golden page. He actually contacted some relatives of mine and he offered me this golden page to write my own answer to this. And I said that I don't want to engage in any kind of correspondence with such unfair and incorrect people and I do not want to engage in correspondence through the press. And I -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, did you mention to him about the fact there might have been incidents, somebody's house blown up, which would generate revenge to kill or mutilate people? It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember having talked to him. Everything that was said had to do with some ethnic questions, really. I don't remember that we talked a lot about Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you mention to him that you were not sure if there were any mass graves?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, Mr. Moore, he was obviously irritated by me when he came and I was simply stunned by his behaviour, a journalist who was there to interview me, based on a recommendation issued by one of my superiors, a General. And he even went as far as to insult me. I can't tell you anything very positive or very negative, I simply can't remember. I'm telling you, this interview is a fabrication, it's entirely made up. He used a lot of phrases and words there that are simply not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, did you mention the fact that you are not sure whether there were any mass graves? Was mass graves mentioned to you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, I remember this encounter and I can't give you a specific answer. I can't tell you that I mentioned this to him or that I didn't. I don't know -- I don't even remember what it was precisely that he asked me, but all I can say is the questions were utterly offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at the next question. "It has been alleged that a mass grave exists two and a half kilometres south-east of the Ovcara farm. People talk about two nights of constant slaughter and about more than 300 people killed among whom were civilians and women. The government of the so-called Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina did not allow the" -- I can't pronounce the word, "and UN experts to investigate there." Now was there any reference to a mass grave existing south-east of the Ovcara farm?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well that appears to be his question but I think he just made it up and made up the answer too along with that. I may have shown him documents about Mitar Karaula at the time to show that these people were still alive. I may have shown him that for all I know, because I was thinking about that. There is a reference to Mitar Karaula. I wanted us to have a man-to-man conversation but he did what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there any mention about a large number of people being murdered in that area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you, we are looking at the figures here, 183 and Mitar Karaula, and I showed him a document with people that this wasn't true, that the people were alive, probably. If you consider the charge that he had against me. I really don't remember. Again, I was telling him that he should bring the questions and that I would write the answers up for him to have the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there any mention about the government?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The answer that you're supposed to have given is, "Why is Ovcara being mentioned? We offered the commander in Mitnica, a certain Mitar Karaula, a free passage for the people and all the guarantees. He came to me and said he wanted us to try him and leave the people alone. I respected his suggestion although he was the greatest criminal. The number of people mentioned (175) is not correct. There were 183 of them, I think. I have the list somewhere. They called us themselves and said: We are the Ustasha army." Well, let's just see about the state of knowledge that you had at the time. Firstly, you've told us that in actual fact there was discussions about Karaula with him; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, if I talk to him, I can't remember talking to a man like that that I talked to. I asked him to bring questions and we could have a proper conversation but he may have insinuated something or other about deaths. And then I gave him, since he mentions a specific figure and the man's name, maybe I showed him the list that very moment and the people who were all alive, as I previously checked, back in 1995, when I said I had read the papers, and that none of those people had come to any harm. But as for all the details with this man who started irritating me the moment I laid eyes on him, I would never have agreed to see him had the General not asked me to. So these are totally arbitrary words, the ones that he used here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I'm dealing with the state of knowledge that you had at the time. "I respected his suggestion although he was the greatest criminal. The number of people mentioned, 175, is not correct. There was 183," but from memory, off the top of my head, I think there were 182. "But the reality is is it was around about that figure, it was just over 180. I think it was 175 troops and 7 officers from memory. So if that's the case, there is only one number out here and that was knowledge you had, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, if I knew, as early as Vukovar, that at Mitnica they surrendered, I'm sorry I can't keep track of every single figure, but I think that 183 armed men had surrendered at Mitnica, that's what I seem to remember. I may have been off by one or two. But this is what I knew in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But in your evidence, not four or five minutes ago, you said, when I was talking about Mitnica, you said, "I think I had a document and that you were going to show it to him. Let's look at what he says in your reply. "There were 183 of them, I think. I have the list somewhere." That's entirely consistent with what you've just told this Court, isn't it, that you had list of them?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't tell him I had the list on me. I still have it. I have a list with 100 -- maybe I should look it up, the documents I provided to my lawyers. Is it 183? Is it 182? I have an individual list of people who were armed when they surrendered at Mitnica in the area of responsibility of the Guards Brigade. I have that list. I had it in Vukovar, I have it today. I had it then too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the question, "But this is about the patients from the Vukovar Hospital." So he's saying: Yes, you're talking about Mitnica, but this inquiry is about the patients from the Vukovar Hospital. It's got nothing to do with Mitnica. And you are supposed to have said: "Let me tell you ... we brought the prisoners to Ovcara. It's a village you know. However, they were protected by the guards and we prevented any massacre of them. They were there for a day or two, I can't remember exactly, and we took from them from there directly to prison in Sremska Mitrovica. Many of them were recently released and all of them in the hospital were taken to Croatia escorted by the EU and other organisations. The Croats returned them on the same day." So, with regard to that answer, there is the reference about, "... and all of them in the hospital were taken to Croatia." Did you ever make that reply about the patients taken from the hospital being taken -- all of them being taken to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, again, I'm telling you these are arbitrary words by a man who tried to talk to me and I told you what it was like. I'm not going into that again. It is with full responsibility that I assert before this Chamber and before you. You should read the Red Cross reports. You should read the ECMM reports. In their reports, they claim that the 400-odd patients from the hospital were evacuated based on an agreement. It's all right there. I don't know why this man wrote what he wrote. If you look at this, this just confirms what I said previously, that I never even suspected that any of the people who were to be exchanged and who had been sent to Ovcara had been killed. I thought it was some civilians coming to grieve but I didn't have the information or anything to indicate that these civilians had come to grief. I simply didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well that cannot be right, with the utmost respect, because your evidence before the break was that you'd been told about bad behaviour at the barracks, and you'd been told about violence at Ovcara. Therefore, there is always the danger, just on a common-sense basis, that something might have gone wrong; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the war itself, and especially this sort of interethnic armed conflict, is the greatest evil that can possibly befall a people. Everybody's armed. Everybody's tense. Everybody's nervous. I gave the examples about our own officers who had suffered mental breakdowns leaving their positions and then ending up at the military hospital academy. This is a great evil but that befell all of us. It just struck us. And you can't expect me to say that everything was fun and games or that everything was ideal. It wasn't. But we did everything we could to prevent any form of riot and any sort of evil happening. Back where I come from, that's how they bring us up. Any misdeeds, any evil deeds, any treason is a curse that will haunt families through generations, and that's what I stick to. I tried to help people and not contribute to the growing amount of misdeeds that were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm going to do is I'm going to go through this question and answer and you can say whether it was said or it wasn't said or whether the topic was touched on; do you understand? And we'll get on much quicker that way. "Monitor, question: You have not been heard about patients being taken at night by buses from Ovcara?" "Sljivancanin: No. They were all taken to the penitentiary in Mitrovica, according to the list. The international organisations have the list and they checked it. Therefore, there were executions by firing squad or killings. Nevertheless, there were corpses which they collected on a heap during cleaning of the city. They were mostly Ustashas. Can you imagine how difficult it was to bury them and, at the same time, decorate them?" Now, was that question never put? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this is an arbitrary random comment made by a man who extrapolated some questions, rephrased them the way he liked them, and then he added something that he wanted there. But I simply don't remember the two of us talking about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Do you know who Arkan is?" Answer: "Yes." Was that asked?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you -- you asked me yesterday but I didn't finish. Please, with all due respect, don't speak ill of the dead. I can't remember us talking about that gentleman, nor was he anywhere near me during our combat missions in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the next question about the fact, "I want you to write this: Arkan's unit did not take place in the liberation of Vukovar or of Borovo Naselje. This has to be distinguished." You didn't say that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he says. Maybe he knew better than I did about Arkan's whereabouts. Arkan may have been in the area, for all I know, but he certainly wasn't in the Guards Brigade, in Borovo Naselje, not with us. He probably had more accurate information to indicate Arkan's whereabouts at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Next question: "That does not make a difference," says he. You allegedly said, "They tried to make contact with us but I did not want to admit anybody who was unwilling to fulfill orders issued by me or my superiors into Operations Group South. As for Arkan himself, I used to ... no, we never met in Vukovar, nor did he come to Vukovar while we were there. Never." Now, this context of Arkan, was that mentioned at all, about him assisting at OG South, or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this gentleman, the journalist, introduced me as a commander, as a great number of media at the time did. But this phrasing, this answer, is something that he made up. The gentleman that you are referring to is dead. I never speak ill of the dead and I certainly never discussed that gentleman with this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal with one aspect of page 3 in the English. There is a large reply after Arkan. It starts: "No, I cannot confirm Arkan's or anybody else's crimes. It is our weak point because we talk about it ourselves. We are constantly looking for quarrels amongst ourselves ... I can only accept what I see in front of me and not what I hear about. For example, the Croatian newspaper Globus claims that the Croatian population considers me the greatest criminal. I could not even have dreamt of what they are now accusing me of. I can talk about Ustasha crimes because I experienced them (for example, they killed my chauffeur). Croats were the ones who started committing atrocities." Did you mention to this journalist about your chauffeur, Mr. Popovic, being killed?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'll answer for the umpteenth time, if that's what it takes: This journalist irritated me the moment he came into the room. We sat there for a brief while. I don't remember telling him about my driver. Maybe he'd read that elsewhere. I did talk often about my driver getting killed. I really felt sorry for him. He was a young man. I'm still sorry. Never fired a bullet, never even carried weapons, and yet he was killed in this ambush. He may have watched some TV programme or read some papers and got the story about my driver from there. But, Mr. Moore, if you insist on quoting this interview - I can't prohibit you from doing that - but I'm telling you it's a fabrication. Most of the questions are made up, most of the answers are simply made up, and I do not acknowledge this interview as one that I actually gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were asked at the bottom: "Sir, are you aware that both Croats and Serbs defended Vukovar? "Sljivancanin: That Serbs defended it, no. They were not Serbs. They were only two Serbs from mixed marriages. They surrendered to me and told me that they had been forcibly mobilised." Was there any reference to that with this journalist that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view was always that Vukovar was defended by all the honourable citizens of Yugoslavia and the JNA included. They had nothing to defend it from. They were just disarming paramilitary formations, because the town belonged to us. But this is not the sort of thing that I shared with any journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've almost finished this document. Next question: "Tell me, why did you raze Vukovar to the ground?" And then there's an answer; I'll read it because, in fairness, it should be done: "We didn't want to destroy Vukovar, but if we want to pursue a military option ... the question was raised as to how to destroy cities, how to destroy your mother country, how to kill your own people with whom you have been friends. But after all instruments were used by Ustasha Croatia, by Europe, and all others to attack the army and the Serbian people, we launched a decisive battle for Vukovar. Let's say that the Ustasha commander Dedakovic came to me and said, listen Sljivo, hey, major, officer, Chetnik. If he had said that, listen, let's talk as human beings, I would have forbidden my troops to fire, but when they killed my chauffeur on the 6th of October, people may say what they like, but I have no mercy towards the Ustashas nor will I ever have." Now, was there any discussion about the Ustasha commander Dedakovic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, again I'm telling you, I, and there was another witness here allegedly P002, who told stories that weren't true. I did speak to Mr. Dedakovic. I said, Let's not kill each other. Let's not keep dying. Let's find a solution. But the journalists wrote whatever they saw fit. Some dramatised the whole thing, some made it out as something rather funny. You know what journalists are like, they just scribble away. And this journalist may have picked up some of that, but I don't remember talking to this gentleman about all these things that he reports. What he says about my driver, this is something that really affected me as a human being, when my driver was killed. It was a difficult time and again, I'm repeating, when we first got to Vukovar, I thought that these people, the people of our town and of our country, once they saw their own army, they would say: This is our own army, don't fire at them. It was a horrible feeling that I experienced when my driver was killed. It's not something I remember, it's just an experience that sticks with you. Well, I don't know, you're reading the answer of a man who you know well, then you should bring the man and talk to him. I don't know what to say, you keep interrupting me. I'm trying to give you my opinion. Why don't you bring this man to Court and he can tell you all about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The next question, "Now what do you think about the defenders of Vukovar?" Now you've mentioned Marin Vidic this morning as being a decent human being, I think. "Sljivancanin: They allowed rascals and hooligans to wage war. When I captured Marin Vidic," so you knew that. "I thought he was somebody. He was the Croatian government's commissioner for Vukovar. When I first saw him, he was nothing but a bum and he was the person who led the Croatian people. He? Well, while we were talking, he drank up a bottle of brandy which I gave him. How can such individuals lead a people towards freedom and democracy." Well, Marin Vidic, you did have dealings with; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this publicly in front of all the world, the world public, everyone, that my talk with Marin Vidic was very respectful. It is true he asked for a drink. He told me how he had been part of an orchestra before, they played the pubs, that sort of thing. He had a glass or two - I didn't keep track - three, perhaps. But would I allow a hooligan to spend the night in the same room as I, the way this journalist makes it out to be? If I stated on the record somewhere that I had had a brandy with Marin Vidic and they made him out to be a hooligan. So that's exactly the sort of words that this dishonourable journalist is using. And I think he should be confronted with this, so I can look him in the eye. Do you think I would have been sitting with Marin Vidic there singing our songs and talking about the things that he wanted to talk about if I had made him to be out like that. There is no need for me to tell any stories about Marin Vidic. What I'm telling you is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move on to the next question, because it deals with Seselj. Remember I asked you questions about Seselj. "Lieutenant Colonel, sir, can Seselj lead another people? Sljivancanin: I don't say he can and I think he never will. Monitor: Don't be too hard. Yesterday you were in Vukovar with him chatting." I asked you yesterday about Vukovar and the memorial service and in fairness to you, you said that you didn't speak to him. But this timing of this article is clearly at a time when it's being suggested by this witness that he saw you at Vukovar and secondly, that Florence Hartmann said she saw you in Vukovar. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, if this is the journalist, you mean he could have not possibly have seen me in Vukovar because he wasn't there. I mean, with Seselj. That means I didn't say yesterday that I didn't see Seselj. I saw him in Vukovar when he came for the second time somewhere near the junction of Prvomajska Street and Nova Street. I can draw that for you if you like. I was on my way back from the Bosko Buha neighbourhood. We passed each other briefly and I told you about all of that. So if he wrote that down, well, then, I said publicly here that I never had any respect whatsoever for Mr. Seselj's political views. I don't think that he's a great politician. I didn't think so then and I don't think so now. If you want me to explain that, I'll be glad to oblige. Secondly, when you have children watching the cartoons just before the evening news, then, you have a granddaughter, for example, she wants to see the news and the granddaughter wants to see the cartoon. And she was watching all the coverage of the assembly where Seselj was staging a ridiculous acts of humour and then the granddaughter would switch to the comics channel and that's what our people used to do. They had to add some humour to our overall experience and to all the things that we were going through, so the granddaughter would then just end up switching to the cartoon channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you were in Vukovar, in November 1992; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, yes, I was, and I explained when it was that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And finally, can I go, please, to the last question: "If the Yugoslav army introduced the traditional Serbian hat and that of the cockade to it as an official insignia, would you put it on your head? Sljivancanin: I would. Why not?" Well, now, Mr. Sljivancanin, was that mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, allow me to explain. This is the greatest fabrication in this interview. Let me tell you something else, too. When I was commander in Podgorica, my late father was dying in hospital. I was notified. I came in to see him and I had the JNA insignia on my cap, the two eagles, I'm not sure what it's called. My father saw me and he was on his deathbed and he said: There you go, my son. You have the eagles up too, don't you? Because that was the sign of the Yugoslav army. He said, you know how much blood has been shed for the five-pointed star to be worn on these caps. This will come to no good at all, we'll never have a country for as long as you keep wearing these. So I was always against the cockade. I'm still against the cockade. And all I can say about your quote, it is a total fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we turn to divider 3 and 4, I'm not going through the details, I don't have time, but there is an interview here on the 29th of November, 1991, literally within a week of the fall of Vukovar. And you can see a photograph of you relaxing in your uniform. Now, this particular interview is an exhibit -- it's Exhibit, I believe, 354. It's headlined "The return of the warrior." Do you accept that this interview occurred?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman who conducted this interview with me was in this courtroom. Everybody examined him. The interview occurred under very peculiar circumstances. On the 24th of November, late in the evening, it may have been between 11.00 and 12.00, I came back, I was tired. I was in a hurry to get home but the journalists pressed and so my superiors had decided, so I briefly talked to them but not nearly as much as they wrote down. Journalists, being what they are, concocted an interview based on this but -- yes, in short, I do remember this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would you say, in general terms, it is accurate?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for me, an interview is accurate when you have a journalist bring questions and I write my answers. Then I can acknowledge that as my interview. If he talks to me first and then writes up the answers however he sees fit, well, those are just random interpretations, totally arbitrary. He adds some, he takes some away. And then the journalist writes down whatever is best for his newspaper at any given time. But I don't agree that maybe in this interview is everything that I said because it wasn't written by my hand, it was written by the hand of the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But did you write in and complain and ask for the golden page to complain?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask at the time what I said about Monitor, the golden page. They were offering me, but I didn't want. And for these, then, when the interview came out the following morning, I talked to journalist Slahovic [phoen] that there he is for you, call him. And I criticised why they had published my photograph on the front page, why they called me at night. I said this was not the least bit respectful and then they offered another interview. Like okay, now we'll give you a new one and then I didn't want any more to talk to, nor did I ever conduct an interview with them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move on from this file. I will make application for the Monitor article to be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit 849.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is the last file that we have. It's called "Belgrade statements", to assist all parties. It's exactly the same format as before, one to four tabs, interview one, one and two, interview 3, interview 2, 3 and 4. To assist the Court and all parties, I hope that you have on the English version a page number on the left-hand side, that is the page number of the B/C/S so that we know where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, the first interview, and I'm going to call them interview for convenience, I don't want to be thought I'm trying to take any advantage of it, but the first interview was 14th of February, 1998. Now, it's tab 2 for you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the interview that took place on the 14th of February, 1998, that was on the premises of the security administration and I think that it lasted all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I just want to deal with is some short issues. There is a date at the very top saying 12th of January. It doesn't say exactly what it refers to. But what I want to know is when or how much before, in time, were you told that they wanted to interview you and that was going to be the 14th of February. So when were you told that you were going to be interviewed? I don't need to know the exact date, just give us an estimate of time.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have to be very exact and precise. I know that and there are no approximations here, Mr. Moore. What I know I want to say exactly. I attended the school of national defence. It was a Saturday morning around 8.00, Saturday. The head of the centre called me in. I came to his office and he said: "Please call the chief of general staff, General Perisic, he wants to talk to you on the telephone." I called and that was say 8.30 or 9.00 that Saturday. General Perisic said to me on the telephone: "Colonel, sir, at 11.00," or at quarter to 11.00, I don't remember exactly, "report to the security administration to General Aca Dmitrijevic, he wants to talk to you about something and I have given my approval for that." So then I reported to General Aca Dmitrijevic and it was then that I first heard from General Aca Dmitrijevic that an interview was supposed to be conducted with me in relation to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can we work on the basis that by 1998 you knew that there was a suggestion that you were involved with others in the murder of people from the hospital and that the murders occurred in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't put it that way. That was not my understanding. I told you in the press there was this indictment that we had been accused. I said that I went to speak to the chief of general staff and that he asked for the matter to be investigated. I imagine he went to the military prosecutor and then I asked to see Mr. Dmitrijevic too but he didn't receive me. When I went to see the General, he said the General would receive me when he would have the time and afterwards, as I was waiting to see what would be done by the military organs in charge, I believed that they would call me when necessary and I was not in a position to take any other measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. It was a very easy question, that is: You, by that time knew, there was an indictment in existence from an International Tribunal and I'm asking, did you know that it related not only to Vukovar but the murder of people from the hospital, the murders at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm giving you my answer. I did not have that indictment in my hands to read specifically what it said, except for what it said in the newspapers. And all newspapers wrote about this any way it suited them. So I was waiting to hear from official organs on the basis of official regulations what it is that I'm being charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you aware that unofficially, there was a suggestion that you were one of a number of people that were responsible for the killings at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that allegedly an indictment had been issued against me, Radic, and Mrksic, that we were being charged for war crimes but with regard to what questions and what it was that we were being charged with, I did not know all of that to tell you the truth, because I did not have the indictment in my own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Never mind the indictment. There are lots of newspapers around. The indictment was 1995, this is 1998. Newspapers are abounded I suggest, with the suggestion that atrocities had occurred at Ovcara. Now, did you know the location was Ovcara or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you now that I heard that it was being talked about, said in various newspapers, but basically I avoided reading newspapers then because one gets so upset when one reads different newspapers and then you see all these different comments in different ways in different newspapers. I was waiting for the official position of the military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that mean, then, that you knew it was Ovcara but you hadn't official confirmation of it? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot agree with that, that that's the way it was. I did not believe that that crime had been committed at all until I came here to The Hague and until I heard what people were saying. I did not believe it. I could not understand that that kind of thing could exist in a human psyche, that people could commit such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is not a case of whether the crimes have been committed. I am asking you again: Did you know or believe or did you believe unofficially, or as a result of unofficial sources, i.e., newspapers, that the atrocities were supposed to have occurred in Ovcara? I'm talking about the location. Whether it was done or whether it wasn't, I'm wanting to know: Did you know about the name Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name Ovcara, as a geographic concept, I knew that from Vukovar when I was there, but I did not believe then that such atrocities and crimes could have been committed as some newspapers wrote. I did not have any information about any such thing having happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you are accepting that newspapers had written that a crime had occurred at Ovcara; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I'm telling you once again: If you're giving the answers then what I said was that I heard stories, I read things, and then I stopped reading because everybody was writing in different ways and commenting in different ways. But I did not know that that crime had been committed until it was confirmed, until an investigation was carried out. I heard about the indictment and then I went to see the responsible people to see why I was being charged with that kind of thing, but I did not know about that crime itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But wasn't it correct that when it came to the content of the interview, that it was perfectly obvious that they were talking about Ovcara? It was mentioned to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ovcara is a geographic concept. It is a settlement, a farm. As far as I knew, while I was in Vukovar, it was a farm, a livestock farm. It also had some kind of administrative part and different rooms where I really never went. I never went there. I wasn't interested in that. And as I said here, my interest as security organ was to deblock the barracks and to disarm the paramilitaries in town itself. In that area, there were no operations going on, it was outside the zone where there was shooting and where there was anything that was going on. So I really wasn't interested in finding out more about Ovcara and I never really stayed there. Perhaps only if I went down the road in a vehicle once to Mitnica and once when I went to see the commander of the 20th Brigade, I don't need to repeat all of that yet again, I already told but that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You certainly discussed Mitnica during this particular interview; isn't that right? And the Mitnica evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent all day talking to the security organs under very complex conditions. Everything I knew, not only about Mitnica, but all the time, while the mission was being carried out, deblocking the barracks and disarming the paramilitary formations, I talked to them about all of that. However, I have to tell you that this is the note they compiled. That is how I understand it. This is not my statement. This was dictated by Colonel -- Colonel -- may I look at the name? May I tell you what the name is? I really forget. My mind seems to stop. Colonel Gajic, yes, he was dictating this to a clerk. When I would talk to him, then he would dictate some sentences to the clerk. But I asked him to give me permission to go and find my papers and to try to remember everything. So it was four years later, no, seven years later that I asked for my reports that I sent to the security administration. He did not allow that, though. He said: All of this is just an initial interview, information, it's not necessary now. When it becomes necessary, we will make all of that possible. I mentioned some names, like representatives of the security administration -- please, let me finish. I have to tell you about this. This is important. I asked for Vasiljevic to be mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I'm sorry, you had a long time with Mr. Lukic where you have explained this. I merely want to ask some questions. Now, what I want to know is, when it came to the interview in Belgrade, it was perfectly clear that the interview was about what happened at Ovcara; that's right, whether it was the Mitnica Battalion or whether it was something else, but that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at that time, the Colonel asked me about all the tasks from the first day of our arrival to have this mission accomplished until our mission was ultimately accomplished. We talked all day about everything, about everything. May I add that he did not allow me to give other names for them to be written down here except for me, Mrksic and Radic because we are like on this indictment and the others don't matter and we will see about that later. I was a bit irritated by that, but what was written was what he had dictated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, what you say is simply not right, because when one looks at the English page 2 at the bottom, there is reference to other names, two lines from the bottom, on your page it's 0218/8349. There is very clear statement on orders from the brigade commander Mile Mrksic, "They were evacuated to Sremska Mitrovica with military trucks in an organised manner and with military escort. On the 18th of November, continuing into the 19th of November, I was personally at Ovcara with Vukasinovic and Karanfilov." So it's not a case of just names of the 3 defendants; there's Karanfilov, there is Vukasinovic and if you want to know there's Borisavljevic, as far as I remember, on the next page. So you were saying that you were at Ovcara on the 18th, 19th, for the Mitnica evacuation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, it is correct that names are mentioned of my men who were with me from the security organs, because this man knew them too; however, I'm trying to say that key names like Vujic, Vasiljevic, and some other commanders are not being mentioned. Especially, at that time, the gentleman suggested to me that it was -- it would not be a good thing to mention them because what I was saying then is what I am saying to you now. He didn't want these names to be mentioned. This is his vocabulary, these are his words, this is his official note, the way he wrote it, from my talk to him. I was at Mitnica or, rather, at Vucedol on the 18th of November with Vukasinovic in order to carry out tasks from the purview of security organs. Now, as for the words written here, this is military vocabulary that he used then. I didn't write this in my own hand. He dictated this to the young lady who was typing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's look at page 8 of the English version. In your page, it's 0218-8352. Now, leading in on page 7, if I may just for the moment, in the English version it's the second paragraph I want to deal with and then turn over the page to page 8. So Mr. Sljivancanin, 0218-8352, "The brigade staff consisting of Panic, Lieutenant Colonel Lukic, Major Bajic and other people whose names I cannot remember, led the further evacuation of the people from the barracks in Vukovar. I do not know what happened in the barracks in Vukovar or how the process of evacuating these people continued." Well, that is not right. You did know what was happening in the barracks. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I am answering you yet again. These are the words that were then deemed necessary by the gentleman who was an official there on behalf of the security organs. He thought that he should write it this way. I talked differently. Perhaps he didn't like the way I talked so he was the one who was dictating the record. At the end, I even got upset. I said, "We are going to stop this. I'm not going to go on any longer. Let me sign this. I want to go and have lunch. I haven't eaten anything all day." It wasn't really a quarrel, but it was sort of a squabble and that's how we ended our conversation. He was the one who was dictating. Now why he dictated this way, I don't know, but I already explained to you, I explained everything to you. I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, if we look on your page halfway down, the English page is page 8, halfway down it starts, "Regarding the allegations in the indictment that 260 persons were shot dead at Ovcara on the 20th of November, and that these were people who had been evacuated from the hospital in Vukovar, I claim that I know nothing about this. I just know that after the completion of the evacuation of the wounded and medical staff from the hospital in Vukovar and my return to the command post, on the evening of the 19th of November. I heard from somebody, perhaps it was Major Vukasinovic, although I am not sure about this, that "it was not nice that they were maltreating these people at Ovcara." So there is a reference to the 20th. There is the reference to the indictment. There is the reference to the people who were killed and there is the reference to Vukasinovic telling you. Now, isn't it right that that was said at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, if we look at this official note very carefully, you will see that I made a mistake with many of the dates there because I didn't have any documents. The first thing that I was primarily guided with was Mr. Vance's visit to Vukovar and the visit of his delegation. I can tell you that I claimed then and that was correct that Mr. Vance was in Vukovar on the 18th. And until I came here to the Detention Unit, until I saw the diaries, because I didn't have any documents then, until I saw the diaries, until the documents were shown here, and the records, I was convinced that Mr. Vance came to Vukovar on the 18th, really. I did not know. I forgot got, quite simply. I knew everything we did, but I did not know the time. I did not know those events. Now, when you read this, I note again the 19th of November. He asked me about the 20th. I said: I don't know about the 20th. And that is where we came to squabble. I kept saying to him -- he asked me how is it that you took people from the hospital on the 20th or, rather, on the 19th when they were killed on the 20th. And I said, I don't know that they were killed. I didn't know that at the time. So that's when we started squabbling about these dates. And then he concluded what he concluded here. I don't know if I mentioned all these names; I cannot remember. But he wrote these names from the Guards Brigade and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Forget about dates. Just remember incidents.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When one looks at this, there is the reference to "It was not nice. They were maltreating those people at Ovcara." So there was a very specific indication of maltreatment of the people at Ovcara. Now, when one reads on about it, it goes on, "As far as I remember, Colonel Mrksic tried to telephone the 80th Brigade to determine what was going on. But the line was -- it says not down but I presume it was down." Then he sent me, Karanfilov, or Vukasinovic and Karanfilov to determine through the brigade command, on the spot, to the Ovcara facility of what was going on. When we arrived there, it was between 2200 and 2230." So the reference is about what was going on vis-a-vis the maltreatment at Ovcara. So never mind the dates. We're talking about the Vukasinovic information which you say was the evening of the 20th, that things were going on. And what you're saying here is Mrksic tried to contact the 80th, couldn't do so, and sent you, Vukasinovic and Karanfilov to find what was going on. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm reading this here now, this note, and he has here in relation to the indictment on the 20th and then he says in the late evening hours, this is allegedly what I'm saying, on the 19th, that I heard that somebody was being maltreated in Ovcara. I testified here that I heard about that on the 19th but not from Vukasinovic, but Mr. Skoric, as I testified here. He is the one who returned these people. What I testified about is correct and here it is also confirmed. You asked me about the hour 20 -- 2300 hours. It pertains to the people who were returned -- who were sent out as a convoy to the Republic of Croatia and then was returned. That was my understanding and as far as I can remember, I was explaining it to the gentleman at that time too that that was it. And no crime suspects are referred to here or prisoners. It is people that is referred to. I remember having said that then. Now, whether he wrote everything down the way I had put it and whether he dictated it properly, well, people make mistakes, don't they. And I said what I had to say and it seems that the time is right here, on the 19th at 2200 hours. Perhaps that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Sljivancanin. The topic of concern was the mistreatment of the people at Ovcara which was coming as a result of the information given by Vukasinovic. And you have told us this morning that Vukasinovic gave that information on the evening of the 20th. It is the incident that is important not the date. Now let's look on at what you say you found: "However, you say you got there and you didn't notice anything special. However, we found Miroljub Vujanovic, a TO commander, with several of his men. When I asked him what was he doing there at the time, Vujanovic answered that he had come to find out what would happen to the vehicles which were there but were originally from Vukovar and that he had come to take these vehicles. I just replied to him that these things regarding the vehicles would be arranged over the following days. We stayed there for ten to 15 minutes at most. We then returned to the command post. I reported to the commander that everything was peaceful at Ovcara." Well, the word "peaceful," might I respectfully suggest to you, does not refer to vehicles. You don't have peaceful vehicles, do you? It refers to the situation at Ovcara, the people?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, that is what my testimony was here, except that I didn't testify about being sent by Commander Mrksic as it is written here. Perhaps the person just wanted to link this up to Mrksic because Vujic and Vasiljevic were being talked about. When I -- in the evening, I came across Vasiljevic in the command and that was not mentioned, but around 2200 hours, when I was at Ovcara on the 19th with Vukasinovic, there was total order, peace, no gunfire was heard, there was nothing that -- I was not talking about peaceful vehicles. Oh, please let me answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sljivancanin, the question was quite specific. The information had come from Vukasinovic about what had happened at Ovcara and you had been sent there by Mrksic along with Vukasinovic and Karanfilov. That's what the question was about. Now, how do you account for that answer and what you have said in evidence today?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, on the 19th, in the evening, Vukasinovic and I went to Ovcara, Karanfilov did not go. This name was put in. I don't know why then, maybe the man made a mistake. I don't remember having mentioned that name because he did not go with me. I don't remember. He really didn't go with me. And everything I said or, rather, everything that is written here for the most part is what I testified about here as to what happened on the 19th and this concerning the vehicles, well, perhaps, written a dit bit differently, but I talked about that to all of you here as well. Well, you are insisting on now that I should tell you, on the 20th, Vukasinovic told me about this evacuation or, rather, that these people being taken away from the barracks to Ovcara. But it wasn't people, these were suspects, crime suspects. And then I'd say that that was that but then he didn't write about that. He didn't write what I said so this term was not presented here in this statement. It was not written. And what happened this time coincides with what I answered you during my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, please look at the end of that document that you have?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Where you refer to "Before a court of my own country and my own people and nowhere else." And it says as follows: "I have nothing else to say and I do not want to read the statement because I listened to the reading of my words which were incorporated in the statement and I hereby sign it without any objections." I would suggest to you, you are an experienced man, you are an officer, but much more importantly, you knew there was an indictment out for you in relation to the killings at Ovcara and you were not going to sign your life away just on some -- if you excuse me -- some hissy fit, because it suited you and you wanted to have lunch. You gave this as a way of trying to get out of your responsibility at Ovcara; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, again, I'm telling you, you keep drawing your own conclusions that I disagree with. I was suddenly summoned to this interview. As a human being and as an officer, I cared, however and how, to tell my story, everything I knew and for all these problems to be resolved and for the truth to finally be known. I didn't shy away from the truth, not when I was on my mission. I spoke to journalists, I spoke to international monitors, I spoke to everyone. I didn't keep them from seeing everything. Wherever I went, they went too. I cared a great deal for all of this to be known, but an altercation ensued between this gentleman and myself because he did not convey my statement faithfully. He mentioned all the persons that he had mentioned and he dictated this statement the way he saw fit. At the end of it all, I said, "I won't read this. Just give it to me to sign." And I've been fooled because that morning when I set out from my home, I hadn't even had breakfast and I was fed up, I just wanted to get my documents and go. I said I would be called again, summoned with my documents to go again and see them but they never called again. And did I care? Yes, I did care for light to be shed on all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Mr. Sljivancanin, you had another interview on the 17th of December of that same year. Now, you say that you had been badly treated in interview, in your first interview. You were then perfectly aware of what the nature of the allegation was so the situation came for an interview in December; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, it wasn't mistreatment but it was certainly disrespectful treatment. They should have made it possible for me to have my papers, have the reports, all the reports that I submitted that I've been trying to show you here for the exact facts and the exact dates to be established for that statement to be authentic. So that's that. As for the 17th of December, as you can see here, I was summoned to go to the military court and I responded to this summons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's very briefly look at this particular interview. You were called to say everything you knew about the case. I'm not going to go through the earlier parts. Now, I want to go, please, to page 6 of the English version, and your page, B/C/S, it is 0218-8293. Now, on that particular page 6 of the English version and on your page, it is the penultimate paragraph and it starts as follows: "That day, on the 18th of November, 1991, at around 1100 hours," well, we know that's the 19th, "Cyrus Vance also came to that sector as a representative of the international community." Then it goes on about things occurring. You say the following: "I stayed with him until 1700 hours." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, this is also --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is right, isn't it, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says 1700 hours. I don't remember actually saying 1700 hours. I didn't stay the whole day. This is something else that the judge dictated. I was giving him my account and he was dictating it to the clerk, the secretary, so the actual words are his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the judge fabricated or was inaccurate about the time of 1700 hours on the 19th of November? That's all I'm asking at this stage.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. I'm not saying that he fabricated this. But 1700 hours, that's nightfall isn't it, that time of the year. I wasn't with Mr. Vance until 1700 hours and I can't say we didn't part before nightfall. I remember that Vance completed his visit around lunchtime and it reads here 1700 hours. I just don't believe I said that because that's dark already, that time of winter. It may be a typo for all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you then say in evidence today that you left Vance around about 2.00, somewhere between that, around 1.00 or 2.00? Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there, even the date is wrong. It was probably me, the 18th, whereas it was the 19th. Well, the date that was misrecorded, I accept that was my mistake because I didn't have any documents to be brutally frank. I remember that we parted ways. According to what I remember, it certainly was at about 2.00 or 1400 hours in the afternoon if you prefer on the 19th, and the date here is wrong on top of that, the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it would have been perfectly possible for you to have been to the yellow house that afternoon on the 19th, that is correct, isn't it, as has been suggested?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, that is simply impossible. I don't think there is any option at all open to allow for the possibility that I was at the yellow house on the afternoon of the 18th. That is entirely impossible. On that afternoon, I was in the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move on, as I say, I've got time constraints. Page 10 of the English. On your page it is 0218-8295. In the page 10 and I'm sorry, I can't be more specific about this, it's towards the bottom of your page about four-fifths of the way down the page. It starts "To understand this better, I would like to point out that the barracks were about three to five kilometres away from the Vukovar Hospital and the large number of citizens were arriving in Vukovar at the time of the evacuation. They were returning because they had previously fled and they were all local people who knew each other and knew who had antagonised whom and who had done what to whom, and since many serious things had happened, there was motive for revenge. So the safest thing to do was to drive them first to the barracks and then secure their transportation from there to Sremska Mitrovica. I am stressing this in particular because I was also in a situation to be exposed not just to insults but even to an assault when I allowed about 24 people from that group to leave." Now, there, you are saying that there was clearly a motive for revenge. Do you accept that that is accurately recorded in relation to motive for revenge?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Moore, I'm telling you the judge was dictating what he was listening to, what I was saying. I did my best as I have explained to explain exactly what had happened. And I'm telling you, throughout the fighting, throughout our attempt to lift the siege on the barracks and the disarming process, we always kept one thing in mind, that the population there was suffering under dire circumstances, that those people were to be comforted, helped. There were certain loose cannons, psychopaths who were creating a lot of trouble. I'm not sure if I should go back to that now. I believe that I told the judge at the time and the judge dictated that in his own words in order to keep the record as short as possible as, the way he saw fit, the way he thought it should be reflected in the record. I didn't see any need to change any of his words. And the representatives of The Hague Tribunal were listening too, both to what I was saying and what the Judge was dictating. But you can't say that it was peaceful because, had it been peaceful, there would have been no need whatsoever for JNA presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you to move on to your page 0218-8297. Before I do it, it's my fault because I was trying to find it and I couldn't, and now I have. Could you just go to 0218-8294, first of all. So 0218-8294, the English version is page 6 at the bottom. So 0218-8294, page 6 in the English. It reads as follows: "I had with me a list of people who organised, together with her, the rebellion in Vukovar. Vidic, Dedakovic, Pol and others, including Bosanac, were on this list." So is it right that you did have a list at that time when you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about that yesterday Mr. Moore, the list that I got from the security administration. I don't remember if I had that list on me at the hospital. Maybe it was on the table in that room. But I had my -- where we stayed. I didn't carry those lists in my pocket all the time, so to speak, but the list that we discussed yesterday I got such lists. I had those for perpetrators of crimes to be found or suspects at any rate, although not all of those were from the Vukovar area but, rather, from the general area as you read out with more detail yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, page 0218-8297, English page 13, going into 14. It is approximately two-fifths of the way down your page. It reads as follows, at the bottom of page 13, English: "While I was in the Vukovar area, after the cessation of fighting and the completion of the evacuation, I was not informed that a group of prisoners were taken to the hangars at the Ovcara farm. I learned about this only later from the media, and it surprised me." Can you assist me on this little point? What about Vukasinovic telling you that in actual fact, there had been a group of people from the hospital and the barracks taken to Ovcara? Because that has been your evidence. And how do you reconcile it with this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I can explain that too. After the interview at the security administration, I asked to find those documents and I was waiting, thinking that I would be summoned for another interview. I phoned the Guards Brigade command since I was no longer an officer of that unit. The then commander of the Guards Brigade told me that he didn't have the documents, nor was there anything he could do about it. He said I should speak to General Panic, who was the commander of the special unit corps. And back in Vukovar, he had been the Chief of Staff of the brigade. So I called Mr. Panic. The General set up an point -- well, I have to tell you, don't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, no. With the utmost of respect to you, the question I would suggest is perfectly clear. What you are saying in this interview is that you did not know about a group of prisoners being taken to Ovcara. I am asking you why are you not saying to the judge, well, I did know about a group of prisoners being taken to Ovcara because Vukasinovic said it to me?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to tell you is what I kept silent about at the time. Back at the military court, I wanted there to be a certain order to this but you are just disrupting me. I went to see Panic. I found Mr. Mrksic there. I wanted to have the documents. Mr. Mrksic then repeated the very same words, he said he had been summoned to the military court too. He said that the government had taken over those people, taken charge of those people. That he would explain in court why that happened and that I and Mr. Radic had nothing whatsoever to do with that. I kept silent in court then, waiting for the commander to speak up about that, since he had a great deal of information of why the people were taken charge of by the government at the time. So I kept silent about that and I told you about how the judge recorded that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that mean, then, you did not tell the truth at your interview on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the whole truth except I kept silent about this final exchange between Mr. Mrksic and myself. I told everything else as I had previously told at the security administration and all of my statements here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is that reply -- does that indicate, the phrase that's used in English, that you were economic with the truth, you only put in that that you wanted?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Moore, I was not being economic with the truth. Everybody knew about it. It was a public session. So I obtained that information from elsewhere, from the commander and from the people that I told you. I expected that it wouldn't be me raising that point in court. I thought Mr. Mrksic would be. The judge didn't ask me. I didn't say anything. And that's how it came to pass and I can hardly come up with a different story now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The last question for this document, page 0218-8298 is yours, the English version is page 15 moving into 16. So for you, 0218-8298, 15/16 for English speakers. Answering a question for the military Prosecutor in Belgrade, the witness stated: "As far as I remember now, I came once to the Ovcara farm with my deputy Vukasinovic to check if the machinery and other vehicles located at the farm had been handed over to the civilian authorities and the Territorial Defence of Vukovar municipality. I'm not sure when this happened and whether this was on the 19th of November or some other day, but I do know that it was sometime in the evening, around about 8.00 p.m.," you say 2000 hours. "And that I found the commander of the 80th Brigade there but I am not sure that it was this unit. This commander informed me that everything was all right there and that the handover of the equipment and the machinery was going on without difficulties. The area of the Ovcara military farm was not in the area of responsibility of our brigade and, therefore, it was not in mine, as the chief of security either. Perhaps the road I was travelling then led me there and I asked about the handover of vehicles and other machinery. I wanted to check this and also draw their attention to prevent any theft of that machinery since there were many cases of looting," and other incidents. So here is a question from the military Prosecutor. You say you've been once to Ovcara and it was only to do with machinery and you were only with Vukasinovic. How do you reconcile that answer with the earlier answer where in actual fact you had been sent by Mrksic to find out what had been going on at Ovcara and you had found Vojinovic not the leader or the officer in charge of the 80th? How do you reconcile those positions and your answers today?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, Mrksic never sent me. I don't remember stating that. I don't remember ever saying that Mrksic sent me to Ovcara. I told you everything that I told you. These are the words of the judge dictating the statement. I repeated to the judge at the time the story that I told here about the mechanisation of other people, what I heard about that and that this occurred on the 19th as agreed. And I believe I said at the time the same thing as I had said previously at the security administration, but that I need to express reservation. There I may have misspoken or something. It is very similar but these are the words of that judge recorded by that secretary. I used my language, the language that I'm using here now. Did he record every single word I said into that record or not, I don't know, but it's very similar. I said that Vukasinovic and I were at Ovcara. There's reference there to mechanisation and everything you're telling me about the officers of the 80th Brigade because we they'd only just arrived. I didn't know a single one of them. I'd never worked with them previously and I didn't know specifically what their names were. I didn't explain to them everything; I didn't give them the entire story as I did at the military court.
