I talked about the 18th, Vucedol and Ovcara, you can go back and read that statement. It's right there. What exactly was it that he eventually dictated just that once, I really don't know. It may have slipped my mind. May have slipped my attention when there were all the questions and answer. Maybe there were omissions in this process of my statement being dictated into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I make application for these statements to be made exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be, Mr. Moore, but we must break now. We've reached the limit of our time, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. It's taken a little longer than I thought. Your Honour, there is only a very small area of evidence that I was going to deal with yesterday. You remember there were video problems. In fairness to Mr. Lukic and Mr. Sljivancanin, I would like to put those matters to him, perhaps, after the break. They will not take more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They can't, Mr. Moore, and I think that means that Mr. Lukic will run out of time today. He may be able to manage. We must break now. We resume at a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic was on his feet following your motion, Mr. Moore. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, I must say I'm actually surprised by Mr. Moore's motion. I think your 16-page written ruling ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Lukic, by chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely why I was surprised that Mr. Moore was raising the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to be continued, not changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've cut my arguments short, I believe, unless you want me to elaborate or unless you think there is anything special that I should add in relation to how I interpret or understand your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore, first, can it be clear what reports or statements you are moving for admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking for the two Belgrade statements to be admissible. I seek to use Rule 89(C). I would submit that that subsection: "A Chamber may admit any relevance evidence which it deems to have probative value." This defendant has given an account, extensively. He has now been cross-examined on the accounts that he gave before the magistrates or the judges and as such, it facilitates a clear understanding by way of comparison and in relation to his credit of the evidence that Mr. Sljivancanin gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You suggest for those reasons that circumstances have now changed from those considered in the decision that was given earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because he has now given evidence. And in relation to that, the Court is entitled to look at that evidence, that account, compare it with the accounts that he has given beforehand, and to assess his credibility in relation to important topics. So in my submission, the ruling was correct initially, but it is the giving of evidence that changes that and modifies it and a court in my submission, and there is provision within the rules, can attach such weight as they deem appropriate to those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Now, Mr. Lukic. I thought I should flesh that out before you spoke. Do you want to add anything further to your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what our position is in it's entirety, Your Honours. I don't think anything's been raised here in relation to our written positions as far as the desire of Mr. Moore was concerned to use these statements in cross-examination and the facts testified to by Mr. Sljivancanin. What you allowed the OTP to do and your understanding of Rule 89 and the case law from the Mucic case that we referred to, when that statement was admitted, that just reinforces our argument from our motion. Your ruling on cross-examination was used and that much is clear. Mr. Moore showed certain segments in his cross-examination to check the credibility. He did that. He did what you required him to do by that decision. None of the facts have changed. We addressed in our motion something that Mr. Sljivancanin addressed in his testimony, how those statements were taken. Those are facts. And you were familiar with those facts when you made that decision; therefore, I think Mr. Moore's new argument brings nothing new to this discussion. It's nothing that you haven't addressed before. Your ruling is very thorough and it thoroughly analyses the arguments proposed by both parties. It is not for me to remind this Trial Chamber that none of the statements were tendered in their entirety; sections were shown and that was evidence. We believe this statement is contrary to the Statute and especially as far as his status before this Court is concerned. I think this would set a precedent in the jurisprudence that has applied throughout this trial so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The motion, Mr. Moore, will be -- the decision on the motion will be reserved and we will evaluate the submissions we've now had. Thank you. Now, you have more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very few. There was a video compiled yesterday that I wanted to deal with the propaganda that existed at that time and we submit is an element that should be taken into account and Mr. Sljivancanin has already indicated that there were certain beliefs, whether erroneous or not. And I would wish to deal with those extractions at the request, indeed, of Mr. Sljivancanin, to show him those video clips if they indeed existed. There are four clips. They are short, and I would wish to play those to him. So may I ask for the first video to be played. Mr. Sljivancanin, this is from the Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with the next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, the next clip I'm going to ask you, please, to consider about lists and the availability of lists to soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, those are four short extracts of material taken from Serbian television in relation to Vukovar. That last extract related to a soldier who was asking about sons. So clearly, the soldier knew, either personally or from something, the names of individuals who were supposed to be fighters against the JNA. Were you ever aware of soldiers being given lists or names of people that they wanted to find?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the clips you've just shown, I watched all the videos that I received when I came here to the Detention Unit. These are all parts of the video set. And as far as I know, with the exception of the bodies outside the hospital, this is all part of the video material in relation to Borovo Naselje. I found out about this while watching this. I am familiar with these. These are dreadful scenes, dreadful imagery. And the last man to be shown wearing a military uniform with a short beard, that's the section I'm talking about, are soldiers, members of the guards unit never got any lists at all. The only exception was what I explained, the lists given to the security officers for intelligence work. That's all they got. The first footage, you called that a JNA soldier giving his account. That's no JNA soldier at all. It's an old man aged over 70. And he is wearing just part of a uniform. Therefore, those who were recording him, the journalists who were creating propaganda for television, since I wasn't an employee of the television myself, could probably shed more light on that, why they recorded it the way they did. There is a lot of material here and I just didn't see that on TV at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I take it then that the bodies that we saw at the hospital, that footage, was the same group of bodies that you said you had seen when you got to Vukovar and had so appalled you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I remember this footage. This is exactly the way I saw bodies lined up and in another street too there were several bodies, when I came on the first day before the Vukovar Hospital. This remained in my memory and the footage shows quite realistically the way it was. I didn't know whether these were bodies of Serbs or Croats or whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to now move and play a video which Mr. Lukic has played but it didn't have a transcript. I think it was Exhibit 839. We have got a transcript which I hope will assist, and the version we are using is V0001411 but the transcript links with that Exhibit 839. If I can just give that transcript out now, please. I wish to play, if I could, please, Exhibit 839, and this is the transcript from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I'm not going to go through the whole video, but the transcript, and we have heard the interpreter about it, he interprets and our translation is the following: "I am very proud to be the commander of these soldiers and officers." Now, this was taken outside the hospital on the 20th; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, in front of the hospital on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have the transcript in his words, Mr. Sljivancanin said he was proud to have been at the helm of, na celu, at the helm of; he did not say that he was the commander. Those were his exact words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We seem to have an interpretation issue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, may I deal with my interpretation and then we can deal with Mr. Lukic's interpretation. I'm quite happy to try and deal with it as best I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you accept that you said that: "I am at the helm of these soldiers and officers"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Moore, I tried many times to explain this to you. As an officer, and as a man, I spoke then before the media, and I had this argument as I had agreed on with Colonel Pavkovic, that after all I do represent a person from the Yugoslav People's Army who is speaking publicly for the media. And I did not want to explain to journalists what duties I had and what it was that I was doing. I did not explain that I was chief of security then, but as I got carried away and at that moment, as I felt things about these young people and that any officer would have been proud to be with such young people, I thought that all soldiers, especially ours from the Guards Brigade, were good people, young people, and that one should be proud to be with these young people. And it's at that moment that I said that I was at the helm of these people. I'm not changing what it was that I thought. I don't want to comment on this. I'm commander, I am commanding. How should I put this? This is sort of a phrase, sort of representation before the public, to put it in the briefest possible terms. It wasn't for me to explain exactly what position I held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But with the utmost respect to you, Mr. Sljivancanin, even with Mr. Lukic's beneficial interpretation that you were at the helm of these soldiers and officers; helm means captain of the ship, doesn't it? That's exactly what it means. In charge.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, it can be interpreted the way you're putting it but I'm just telling you at that moment, as the representative of the army, I was speaking in order to refute what Mr. Moore was saying. At the request of Mr. Martin Bell, I felt then that I was representing the Yugoslav People's Army and the public would hear it and that is what I said at the time as the representative of the army which, in my opinion, at that time, was honourable and honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On the second page of the English version, you repeat the commander element. It's halfway down the English version. It's one word in. "I told this gentleman this morning that I was the commander in my homeland, in my country." Now, I think in fairness to you, we will play all of the video up to that and we'll hear what the interpreter also says. So if that could be done, I would be very grateful. So shall we start from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I may be of assistance. Let me not challenge so that we don't have to watch the entire video that that is indeed what it says on the second page. "I'm commander in my own country." I mean I want to speed up the proceedings. It's on the second page, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that in actual fact, you were not only de jure commander at the hospital and elsewhere, you were the de facto commander. And secondly, you were the chief of the security organ, the zone of the responsibility of the Guards Motorised Brigade at the least, was not only from the hospital but also the barracks, and I'm suggesting you knew perfectly well that you were part of the structure of OG South and your zone of responsibility included Ovcara. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, really, with all due respect, I do not accept that but I am telling you the following: This word that I said to this man, this -- I met Mr. Borsinger, and there is video footage of what I said to him but then it just came out of my mouth and in front of the journalists. Because I was not very good at this, dealing with journalists. Then I repeated other words. I did not know how to say those words about the death of the young soldiers. It just came out because of exhaustion and because of the killing of these young men. I was chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade and as a professional organ of the command of that brigade, with regard to state security matters, I tried, to the best of my ability, to conduct my duties professionally and correctly and I do not agree that I had any kind of command function de jure and de facto. It says in the rules and regulations what I was and also in my personal files and documents you have exact information as to what duties I held, what I was, and what I did. That is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you, Mr. Sljivancanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Clearly, we should now break for the day and continue tomorrow, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just deal with one small matter. I didn't make an application to put in what I call the propaganda videos. Might I make an application for that to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The four clips will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the four clips will become Exhibit 850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We resume tomorrow at 10.00. May I thank, in particular, the -- those supporting the court, in particular, the interpreters for the unusual time we extended the sessions this morning to try and ensure the proper flow of the evidence and the -- what I thought was to be the end of the cross-examination at the end of the last session. With those words of thanks, we adjourn for the day to resume tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of November, 2006, at 10.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
